topics.title: The microscope and the rules of working with it. Preparing temporary slides. Viruses. Prokaryotic and eukaryotic cells, their structure and differences

goals.text: To teach the student the tasks of biology and the main properties of life, the cell theory, the structure of the light and electron microscope and the rules of working with them, the technique of preparing a temporary slide, and the structure and medical importance of the non-cellular (viruses) and cellular (prokaryotic and eukaryotic) forms of life.
By the end of the class the student should know:

items: the main properties of life and its levels of organization;
the main statements of the cell theory and the methods of studying the cell;
the mechanical, optical and illuminating parts of the light microscope and the types of microscopes;
the structure and reproduction of viruses and bacteriophages and the diseases they cause;
the main differences between prokaryotic and eukaryotic cells.

goals.text: The student should be able to:

items: set up the microscope and examine a slide under the low-power and high-power objective;
calculate the total magnification;
prepare a temporary slide (onion skin epidermis);
recognize and correct mistakes made while working with the microscope.

sections.title: 1. Biology and the main properties of life

blocks.text: **Biology** (Greek *bios* — life, *logos* — science) is the science that studies all manifestations of life: the structure, function, development and origin of organisms and their relationships with each other and with the environment. The term was introduced independently by J.B. Lamarck and G. Treviranus at the beginning of the XIX century. **Medical biology** studies the human body as a biological object and is the foundation for histology, physiology, biochemistry, microbiology, pathology and the clinical sciences.

Biology uses **observation, description, comparison, experiment, the historical method, modeling** and **statistical** methods. Living nature differs from non-living nature by the following set of properties:

blocks.text: Levels of organization of life

items: **Molecular-genetic** — nucleic acids and proteins; storing and transmitting hereditary information.
**Cellular** — the cell is the smallest structural and functional unit of life.
**Tissue and organ** — groups of specialized cells in multicellular organisms.
**Organism (ontogenetic)** — the whole individual and its development.
**Population-species** — a group of freely interbreeding individuals of a species; the elementary unit of evolution.
**Biogeocenotic and biosphere** — exchange of matter and energy between organisms and the environment.

parts.text: Order of the levels: **“My Cat Takes Only Pure Biscuits”** — Molecule, Cell, Tissue, Organism, Population, Biosphere.

sections.title: 2. The cell theory and methods of studying the cell

blocks.text: The cell was first seen in 1665 by the English scientist **R. Hooke** in a section of cork; he called it a “cell”. **A. Leeuwenhoek** observed unicellular organisms, erythrocytes and spermatozoa; **R. Brown** discovered the nucleus in 1831. In 1838–1839 **M. Schleiden** and **T. Schwann** created the cell theory, and in 1858 **R. Virchow** added the statement “Every cell comes only from a cell” (*Omnis cellula e cellula*).
Main statements of the modern cell theory

items: The cell is the elementary unit of structure, function and development of life.
The cells of all organisms are similar (homologous) in structure, chemical composition and life processes.
Cells reproduce only by division of a mother cell.
In a multicellular organism cells unite into tissues and organs and form an integrated system.
The cells of an organism are totipotent — all cells contain the same genetic information, but different genes are active in them (differentiation).

blocks.text: The light microscope consists of **mechanical**, **optical** and **illuminating** parts (Figure 1.1). The mechanical part holds all the parts together, moves the slide and adjusts the focus; the optical part magnifies the image; the illuminating part directs the light onto the slide.

blocks.text: **Total magnification** = eyepiece magnification × objective magnification. For example, with a ×10 eyepiece and a ×40 objective the object is magnified 400 times. The ×90 objective is an **immersion** objective: a drop of **cedar (immersion) oil**, whose refractive index is close to that of glass, is placed between the slide and the objective.

The quality of a microscope is determined not by its magnification but by its **resolving power** — the smallest distance at which two points are still seen as separate. In the light microscope it is about half the wavelength of light (≈ 0.2 µm); therefore small structures such as ribosomes and membranes are visible only in the electron microscope.

sections.title: 4. Rules of working with the microscope

items: Lift the microscope holding the arm with the right hand and the base with the left; place it 3–5 cm from the edge of the table with the arm facing you.
Turn the nosepiece to put the **low-power objective (×8 or ×10)** in the center until it clicks.

Raise the condenser and open the diaphragm. Looking into the eyepiece, turn the mirror until the field of view is evenly lit (with artificial light use the flat side of the mirror, with daylight — the concave side).
Put the slide on the stage with the coverslip facing up, fix it with the clips and bring the area to be studied under the objective.

Looking from the side, lower the objective with the coarse adjustment knob to 0.5 cm above the slide; then, looking into the eyepiece, turn the knob **away from yourself** (raising the tube) until a clear image appears.

Bring the area of interest to the center of the field and switch the nosepiece to the **high-power objective (×40)**; sharpen the image only with the **fine adjustment knob** (turning it no more than half a turn).
After work put the low-power objective in place, remove the slide, wipe the microscope with a soft cloth and put it in its case.

parts.text: The **coarse adjustment knob** must not be used with the high-power objective: its working distance is about 0.6 mm, so it touches the slide, breaks the coverslip and damages the lens. Do not wipe lenses with your fingers or with paper.

blocks.text: **Drawing rule:** the slide is viewed with the left eye while both eyes stay open; the drawing is made with the right hand in an album with a simple pencil, the parts are named with pointer lines, and the name of the slide and the magnification are written under the drawing.

A **temporary slide** is prepared in a drop of water, glycerol or saline for viewing during one class; it dries quickly and cannot be stored for long. A **permanent slide** is prepared by fixing the tissue, dehydrating it, embedding it in paraffin, cutting it on a microtome into sections 5–7 µm thick, staining it (for example, with hematoxylin and eosin) and mounting it under Canada balsam; it can be kept for many years.
Preparing a temporary slide of onion skin epidermis

items: Place 1 drop of water in the middle of a clean glass slide with a pipette.
With forceps peel a thin, transparent film of epidermis from the inner concave surface of an onion scale.
Spread the film in the drop, making sure it does not fold.
Touch the drop with the coverslip held at an angle of 45° and lower it slowly — this way no air bubbles remain.

Remove the excess water with filter paper; if needed, put a drop of iodine solution at the edge of the coverslip and draw it under with filter paper from the opposite side (the nucleus stains yellow-brown).
Examine the slide first under low power and then under high power, and draw the cell wall, cytoplasm, nucleus and vacuole.

parts.text: Round “cells” with a thick black rim on a slide are often **air bubbles**: when the focus knob is turned, their black rim widens and narrows, while a real cell shows an internal structure (the nucleus).

sections.title: 6. The non-cellular form of life — viruses and bacteriophages

blocks.text: Viruses were discovered in 1892 by the Russian scientist **D.I. Ivanovsky** while studying tobacco mosaic disease. Viruses are **obligate intracellular parasites** 20–300 nm in size that reproduce only inside living cells. Outside the cell (as a virion) they show no properties of life, but after entering a cell they carry out their own genetic program; that is why they are regarded as a form between living and non-living nature.

blocks.label: Figure 1.2
blocks.caption: Viruses of various shapes: herpes virus (icosahedral capsid and envelope), influenza virus (helical nucleocapsid and envelope), tobacco mosaic virus (helical symmetry) and a bacteriophage (complex symmetry) (P.Kh. Kholikov et al., 2022).

blocks.text: Structure of a virus

items: **Nucleic acid** (the genome) — either DNA or RNA (never both); single- or double-stranded.
**Capsid** — the protein coat surrounding the nucleic acid; built of capsomeres. Nucleic acid + capsid = **nucleocapsid**.
**Envelope** (supercapsid) — in complex viruses, a lipoprotein membrane taken from the host cell membrane, carrying glycoprotein “spikes” (influenza, HIV, herpes).
Some viruses carry enzymes: for example, HIV has **reverse transcriptase**, which makes a DNA copy of RNA.

blocks.text: Reproduction of a virus in the cell

items: **Adsorption** — the virus binds to a specific receptor on the cell surface.
**Entry** — by endocytosis or membrane fusion; a bacteriophage injects only its nucleic acid.
**Uncoating** — the capsid breaks down and the genome is released.
**Synthesis** — viral nucleic acid and proteins are made using the cell’s machinery.
**Assembly** — new virions are formed.
**Release** — by lysis of the cell or by budding.

blocks.text: **Bacteriophages** (phages) are viruses that parasitize bacteria; they were discovered in 1917 by F. d’Hérelle. A phage consists of a head (DNA inside an icosahedral capsid), a tail (a contractile sheath and an inner tube), a base plate and tail fibers (Figure 1.3). **Virulent** phages lyse the bacterium; **temperate** phages insert their DNA into the bacterial chromosome (a prophage), produce lysogeny and carry genes in transduction. Phages are used to treat intestinal infections (phage therapy) and to type bacteria.

blocks.label: Figure 1.3
blocks.caption: Structure of a bacteriophage: head (DNA inside the capsid), tail, base plate and tail fibers; on the right — phages attached to the surface of a bacterium as seen in the electron microscope (P.Kh. Kholikov et al., 2022).

parts.text: Antibiotics do not act on viruses because viruses have no cell wall, no ribosomes and no metabolism of their own. The main measures against viral infections are **vaccination** and **antiviral drugs** acting on the stages of viral reproduction (for example, reverse transcriptase inhibitors in HIV infection).

blocks.text: Cellular organisms are divided into two groups. **Prokaryotes** (*pro* — before, *karyon* — nucleus) are bacteria and archaea without a formed nucleus. **Eukaryotes** are the cells of fungi, plants, animals and humans that have a true nucleus.

A **bacterial cell** is 0.5–5 µm in size. It consists of a cell wall (peptidoglycan — murein), sometimes a capsule, the cytoplasmic membrane and its folds — **mesosomes**, cytoplasm, **70S ribosomes**, a **nucleoid** (a single circular DNA molecule) and **plasmids** (additional small circular DNA). Most have flagella and pili (fimbriae). By shape, cocci, rods (bacilli), vibrios and spirilla are distinguished. Bacteria reproduce by **binary fission**; under favorable conditions they divide every 20–30 minutes. Under unfavorable conditions some of them form **spores**.

**Mycoplasmas** are the smallest free-living prokaryotes, 0.1–0.3 µm in size, without a cell wall; their shape is variable and they are not sensitive to penicillin (they cause pneumonia and urogenital infections).

cases.title: Case 1
cases.text: A student saw the slide well under the low-power objective, then switched the nosepiece to the high-power objective, but the image disappeared.
cases.ask: What are the possible causes, and how should they be corrected?
cases.answer: Causes: (1) the area of interest was not brought to the center of the field — the field of the high-power objective is much narrower; (2) the slide is upside down (coverslip facing down), so the high-power objective cannot reach focus; (3) there is not enough light — with the high-power objective the diaphragm must be opened and the condenser raised; (4) the objective was not turned until it clicked into place. Correction: return to the low-power objective, center the area, place the slide correctly, increase the light and adjust only with the fine knob.

cases.title: Case 2
cases.text: A student broke the coverslip while working with the high-power objective.
cases.ask: What mistake was made?
cases.answer: The sharpness under the high-power objective was adjusted with the coarse knob: the working distance of this objective is very small (≈ 0.6 mm), so with the coarse knob the tube drops sharply and the objective hits the slide. The slide may also have been placed upside down. The correct way is to use only the fine adjustment knob with the high-power objective and to bring the objective close to the slide while looking from the side.

cases.title: Case 3
cases.text: In a light microscope slide, cells were seen whose flattened nucleus was pressed to the edge of the cell and whose cytoplasm consisted of one large cavity.
cases.ask: What cell could this be? Why is the nucleus pushed to the edge?
cases.answer: This could be a fat cell (adipocyte) or a mature plant cell with a large central vacuole. In an adipocyte almost all the cytoplasm is occupied by a single large fat droplet; in a plant cell, by the central vacuole filled with cell sap. In both cases the large inclusion or vacuole presses the nucleus and the cytoplasm against the cell wall (to the periphery).

goals.text: To teach the student the chemical composition of the eukaryotic cell, the ultrastructure and functions of the general and special organelles and of inclusions, the structure of the nucleus and chromosomes, the structural model of the biological membrane and the mechanisms of transport of substances across it, and the medical importance of solutions.

sections.title: 1. General structure and chemical composition of the eukaryotic cell

blocks.text: Eukaryotes include unicellular protozoa, fungi, plants and animals. A eukaryotic cell has three main parts: the **plasma membrane** (cell envelope), the **cytoplasm** (hyaloplasm, organelles and inclusions) and the **nucleus**. Human cells range in size from 7–8 µm (erythrocyte) to 150 µm (egg cell), and their shape depends on their function: spherical, flat, cuboidal, prismatic, stellate, with processes (neuron).

blocks.text: **Water** makes up 70–80 % of the cell mass. It is the universal solvent, the medium and a participant of chemical reactions (hydrolysis), a regulator of heat and a means of transporting substances. **Mineral salts** in the form of ions are needed for the membrane potential (K^+^, Na^+^, Cl^−^), buffering (HPO~4~^2−^, HCO~3~^−^), blood clotting and muscle contraction (Ca^2+^).

blocks.text: Proteins are **simple** (made only of amino acids: albumins, globulins) and **complex** (protein + non-protein part: glycoproteins, lipoproteins, nucleoproteins, chromoproteins such as hemoglobin). Disruption of the natural structure of a protein is called **denaturation**.

sections.title: 2. The plasma membrane: structure and functions

blocks.text: The cell envelope consists of the **plasmalemma** (the main part) and the **glycocalyx** on its outer surface (carbohydrate chains of glycoproteins and glycolipids). In plant cells there is a cellulose cell wall outside the plasmalemma.

In the electron microscope the membrane appears as a three-layered (dark–light–dark) structure 7.5–10 nm thick and is called the **universal elementary biological membrane**. According to the modern **fluid mosaic model** (S. Singer and G. Nicolson, 1972), the basis of the membrane is a **phospholipid bilayer**: the hydrophilic “heads” face outward and the hydrophobic “tails” face inward. **Integral** (fully embedded, spanning the membrane), **semi-integral** and **peripheral** (lying on the surface) proteins are arranged in the lipid layer like a mosaic and can move laterally (Figure 2.1). Cholesterol regulates the fluidity of the membrane.

blocks.label: Figure 2.1
blocks.caption: Structure of the plasma membrane (fluid mosaic model): phospholipid bilayer, integral and peripheral proteins, cholesterol, carbohydrate chains of glycoproteins (glycocalyx) and cytoskeletal filaments (P.Kh. Kholikov et al., 2022).

blocks.text: Main functions of the plasmalemma

items: **Barrier** — separates the internal environment of the cell from the external one;
**Transport** — passes substances selectively;
**Receptor** — recognizes hormones, mediators and antigens (glycocalyx);
**Intercellular communication** — forms contacts (desmosomes, tight and gap junctions);
**Enzymatic** — membrane-bound enzymes (for example, in the intestinal epithelium);
**Electrogenic** — creates the membrane potential and conducts the nerve impulse.

blocks.text: The **sodium-potassium pump** (Na^+^/K^+^-ATPase) removes 3 Na^+^ ions from the cell and brings 2 K^+^ ions into it for each ATP molecule (Figure 2.2). As a result there is much K^+^ inside the cell and much Na^+^ outside; this is the basis of the **resting membrane potential**, of maintaining cell volume and of secondary active transport. Up to one third of the energy used by the body goes into the work of this pump.

parts.text: Solutions given intravenously are mainly **isotonic** (0.9 % NaCl, 5 % glucose). **Hypertonic** solutions (10 % NaCl) are used to clean purulent wounds (they draw water from the wound) and magnesium sulfate as a laxative, while **hypotonic** solutions are used with caution in some states of dehydration.

blocks.text: The **cytoplasm** is the part of the cell between the plasmalemma and the nucleus. It consists of the **hyaloplasm** (cytosol — a colloidal solution rich in proteins, enzymes and ions), **organelles** (permanent structures with a definite function) and **inclusions** (temporary structures). Organelles are **general** (in all cells) and **special** (in some specialized cells); general organelles are in turn divided into membrane-bound and non-membrane groups.

blocks.text: **Special organelles:** cilia and flagella (axoneme — 9 peripheral pairs + 2 central microtubules, “9 + 2”), myofibrils (contraction in muscle cells), neurofibrils (in neurons), tonofibrils (in epithelium), microvilli (increase the absorptive surface of the intestinal epithelium).

parts.text: In a hereditary defect of the ciliary protein dynein (**Kartagener syndrome**) clearance of the airways is impaired (chronic bronchitis, sinusitis), spermatozoa are immotile (infertility), and reversed position of the organs is often seen.

blocks.text: **Inclusions** are structures that appear and disappear as a result of cell activity: **trophic** (glycogen, fat droplets, protein granules), **secretory** (secretory granules), **excretory** (substances to be removed), **pigment** (melanin, hemoglobin, lipofuscin — the “aging pigment”).

The **nucleus** is the center that stores hereditary information and controls the activity of the cell. The interphase nucleus consists of (Figure 2.4): the **nuclear envelope** (karyolemma — two membranes, the perinuclear space and **nuclear pores**; the outer membrane continues into the ER), the **karyoplasm** (nuclear sap), **chromatin** and the **nucleolus** (where rRNA is synthesized and ribosomal subunits are assembled). Cells without a nucleus (mature erythrocytes) do not divide and do not live long.

blocks.label: Figure 2.4
blocks.caption: Structure of the nucleus: nuclear envelope and pores, chromatin, nucleolus, rough endoplasmic reticulum with ribosomes (P.Kh. Kholikov et al., 2022).

blocks.text: **Chromatin** is a complex of DNA and histone proteins. Its densely staining, inactive part is called **heterochromatin**, and its lightly staining, active (transcribed) part — **euchromatin**. DNA winds around histones to form **nucleosomes** and then coils step by step, turning into compact **chromosomes** during mitosis.

A **metaphase chromosome** consists of two **chromatids** joined at the primary constriction — the **centromere**. The centromere divides the chromosome into two **arms**; the ends of the arms are **telomeres**. Some chromosomes have a secondary constriction and a **satellite**.

cases.title: Case 1
cases.text: Blood taken from a patient was placed in a solution. In the slide prepared from it, the blood cells had a shrunken (crenated) shape.
cases.ask: Explain the situation.
cases.answer: The blood was placed in a hypertonic solution (NaCl concentration above 0.9 %). According to the law of osmosis, water moves from the less concentrated medium (inside the erythrocyte) to the more concentrated medium (the outer solution); the cell volume decreases and it shrinks — plasmolysis (in erythrocytes — crenation). That is why large volumes of hypertonic solutions must not be given intravenously.

cases.title: Case 2
cases.text: Blood taken from a patient was placed in a solution. In the slide, the blood cells were swollen and burst.
cases.ask: Explain the situation.
cases.answer: The blood was placed in a hypotonic solution (for example, distilled water). Water enters the erythrocyte, the cell swells, the membrane stretches and bursts, and hemoglobin escapes — hemolysis. Therefore isotonic (0.9 %) NaCl, not distilled water, is used to dilute drug solutions.

cases.title: Case 3
cases.text: An electron micrograph of liver cells showed marked enlargement and increase of the smooth endoplasmic reticulum. The patient had been taking barbiturates for a long time.
cases.ask: What is this change related to?
cases.answer: The enzymes that detoxify drugs and poisons (the cytochrome P450 system) are located in the membranes of the smooth ER. With long-term intake of barbiturates these enzymes are induced, and the smooth ER that contains them enlarges as well. As a result drugs are broken down faster — tolerance to the drug develops.

sections.title: 1. The life cycle and mitotic cycle of the cell

blocks.text: The **life cycle** is the period from the moment a cell appears by division until it divides itself or dies. It includes growth, differentiation, performance of a specialized function and aging. The **mitotic (cell) cycle** is the period of preparation for division (interphase) and of division (mitosis); it occurs only in dividing cells (Figure 3.1).

blocks.label: Figure 3.1
blocks.caption: Stages of the cell cycle: interphase (G~1~ — growth, S — DNA replication, G~2~ — preparation for division) and mitosis (prophase, metaphase, anaphase, telophase) followed by cytokinesis (P.Kh. Kholikov et al., 2022).

Genetic formula
rows: The cell grows; RNA, proteins and organelles are synthesized; enzymes for the S period accumulate

blocks.text: Interphase may be **autosynthetic** (the cell prepares to divide) or **heterosynthetic** (the cell makes products for the organism and performs a specialized task). The cycle is controlled at **checkpoints** (G~1~/S, G~2~/M and the metaphase checkpoint) through cyclins and cyclin-dependent kinases; if DNA is damaged, the **p53** protein stops the cycle or starts apoptosis.

blocks.text: **Mitosis** (indirect division) is the main way somatic cells divide; it produces two daughter cells genetically identical to the mother cell. Mitosis consists of four phases and is followed by division of the cytoplasm — **cytokinesis**.

blocks.title: Table 3.3. Phases of mitosis
head: Phase
Processes
Genetic formula
rows: Chromosomes coil and become visible; the nucleolus and nuclear envelope disappear; centrioles move to the poles, the spindle forms
Spindle fibers attach to the kinetochores, chromosomes move toward the equator
Chromosomes lie in the equatorial plane and form the **metaphase plate**; they are most condensed — the best time to study the karyotype
Centromeres divide, chromatids (daughter chromosomes) are pulled to opposite poles
Chromosomes uncoil at the poles, the nuclear envelope and nucleolus re-form; cytokinesis

blocks.label: Figure 3.2
blocks.caption: Formation of the spindle in metaphase: centrioles at the poles, astral rays and spindle fibers radiating from them, and chromosomes at the equator (P.Kh. Kholikov et al., 2022).

blocks.text: In an animal cell cytokinesis proceeds by a **cleavage furrow** (contraction of an actin-myosin ring), and in a plant cell by formation of a **phragmoplast** and a cell plate in the middle of the cell. Higher plants have no centrioles, but a spindle still forms (without astral rays — “anastral” mitosis).

parts.text: Order of the phases: **“PMAT — Please Make A Team”**: chromosomes **P**ack (coil), **M**eet in the middle, **A**part they go, **T**wo nuclei form.

blocks.text: Biological and medical importance of mitosis

items: Ensures equal distribution of hereditary information to daughter cells and constancy of the karyotype;
Underlies growth of the organism and renewal and regeneration of tissues;
Is the cytological basis of asexual reproduction.
Failure of mitotic control leads to **tumors**; many anticancer drugs (colchicine, vincristine, taxanes) stop mitosis by acting on the spindle.

sections.title: 3. Other forms of division and pathology of mitosis

head: Form
Essence
Where it occurs
rows: The nucleus divides by constriction, no chromosomes or spindle form; hereditary material is divided unequally
Aging and inflamed tissues, tumors, the macronucleus of ciliates
Chromosomes double without breakdown of the nuclear envelope, no cytokinesis — a **polyploid** cell
Chromatids replicate many times but do not separate — **giant (polytene) chromosomes**

blocks.text: **Pathology of mitosis** includes unequal separation of chromosomes to the poles (**nondisjunction**), tripolar or multipolar mitoses, lagging of chromosomes at the equator, and loss of the spindle under colchicine (**C-mitosis**). In somatic cells such errors cause **mosaicism** (two or more cell lines with different karyotypes in one organism) and **aneuploidy** in tumor cells.

parts.text: **Apoptosis** is programmed cell death: the cell shrinks, chromatin condenses and fragments, the cell breaks into apoptotic bodies and is phagocytosed without inflammation. It is important in embryogenesis (removal of the tissue between the fingers) and in eliminating damaged and tumor cells; its weakening leads to tumors and its excess to neurodegenerative diseases.

blocks.text: **Meiosis** is the division that occurs during maturation of sex cells (gametes) and halves the number of chromosomes. After a single DNA replication there are **two divisions** in a row (meiosis I and meiosis II), and four haploid (n) cells are formed from one diploid (2n) cell (Figure 3.3).

blocks.label: Figure 3.3
blocks.caption: Stages of meiotic division: meiosis I (prophase I, metaphase I, anaphase I, telophase I) and meiosis II (prophase II, metaphase II, anaphase II, telophase II) (P.Kh. Kholikov et al., 2022).

blocks.text: Meiosis I — the reductional division

blocks.title: Table 3.5. Stages of prophase I
head: Stage
Process
rows: Chromosomes appear as thin long threads
Chromosomes thicken; segments are exchanged between chromatids of homologous chromosomes — **crossing over**
Homologs begin to move apart, chiasmata (crossing points) become visible; human oocytes stop at this stage (dictyotene) for years
Chromosomes are maximally condensed, the nucleolus and nuclear envelope disappear

items: **Metaphase I** — bivalents lie at the equator (the homologs of each pair face opposite poles) — 2n4c.

**Anaphase I** — not chromatids but **whole homologous chromosomes** (each with two chromatids) are pulled to the poles; the separation of each pair is independent of the other pairs — 1n2c at each pole.
**Telophase I** — two cells form in which the chromosome number is haploid but each chromosome has two chromatids (n2c).

blocks.text: **Interkinesis** is the short period between meiosis I and II; there is **no** DNA replication in it.
Meiosis II — the equational division

Meiosis II proceeds like mitosis: in metaphase II chromosomes lie at the equator, in anaphase II centromeres divide and chromatids move to the poles. As a result four haploid cells (1n1c) are formed. It differs from mitosis in that the chromosome number is haploid and there is no DNA synthesis before the division.

parts.text: Meiosis has **three sources** of genetic diversity: (1) crossing over; (2) independent assortment of homologous pairs in metaphase I — more than 2^23^ combinations in humans; (3) random fusion of gametes at fertilization. That is why brothers and sisters (except identical twins) are never completely alike.

**Nondisjunction** of chromosomes in meiosis produces disomic (n + 1) and nullisomic (n − 1) gametes. When they fuse with a normal gamete, **trisomy** (Down — 47,XX,+21; Klinefelter — 47,XXY) or **monosomy** (Shereshevsky-Turner — 45,X) develops. The risk of nondisjunction rises with maternal age because oocytes remain arrested in diplotene for many years.

blocks.text: **Asexual reproduction** involves one parent, takes place without gametes and is based on mitosis; the offspring is a genetic copy (**clone**) of the parent. In **sexual reproduction** gametes from two parents fuse; the genetic diversity of the offspring increases, which ensures adaptation to a changing environment.

cases.title: Case 1
cases.text: The genetic material of a group of cells was studied and found to be 2n2c. After division, some cells had a DNA content of 2c and others 1c.
cases.ask: By what method did these cells divide?
cases.answer: Formation of 2c daughter cells is typical of mitosis: a 2n2c cell becomes 2n4c in the S period and after mitosis gives two 2n2c cells. Cells with 1c are formed after the second division of meiosis (1n1c). Thus some of the cells in the group divided by mitosis and others by meiosis (gametogenesis).

cases.title: Case 2
cases.text: Under the action of a harmful factor, spindle fibers did not form in a cell.
cases.ask: Which processes are disturbed, and what is the result?
cases.answer: Without spindle fibers, chromosomes cannot gather on the metaphase plate and are not distributed to the poles in anaphase; mitosis stops in metaphase (C-mitosis). If the cell then re-forms the nuclear envelope, a polyploid (4n) cell with a doubled chromosome number appears. This principle is used with colchicine in karyotype analysis and to obtain polyploid plants, and with vincristine to treat tumors.

cases.title: Case 3
cases.text: Sex cells were found to contain more chromosomes than normal.
cases.ask: Which periods of meiosis may have been disturbed, and what is the consequence?
cases.answer: The cause is nondisjunction of a pair of homologous chromosomes in anaphase I (n + 1 and n − 1 gametes) or nondisjunction of sister chromatids in anaphase II. When a disomic (n + 1) gamete fuses with a normal gamete, trisomy (47 chromosomes) results: for pair 21 — Down syndrome, XXY — Klinefelter syndrome. A nullisomic gamete gives monosomy (45,X — Shereshevsky-Turner syndrome).

blocks.text: **Genetics** is the science of the laws of heredity and variability of organisms. Its founder is the Czech scientist **G. Mendel**, who announced the laws of inheritance in 1865 on the basis of his experiments with peas. These laws were rediscovered in 1900 by H. de Vries, C. Correns and E. Tschermak; the term “genetics” was introduced by W. Bateson in 1906. Later stages: T. Morgan’s chromosome theory, the DNA model of J. Watson and F. Crick (1953), the discovery of the genetic code, genetic engineering and the reading of the human genome (2003).

Definition
rows: A segment of DNA that determines the structure of a particular protein or RNA; the unit of heredity
The position of a gene on a chromosome

blocks.text: **Rules of notation:** P — parents, ♀ — female, ♂ — male, × — cross, G — gametes, F~1~, F~2~ — first and second generation hybrids. The female organism is written first. In human genetics the marriage of parents is also shown with “×”.

The main conditions of the **hybridological method** used by Mendel: pure lines (homozygotes) were chosen, clearly contrasting alternative traits were observed, and each generation was analyzed separately and quantitatively (statistically).

sections.title: 2. Monohybrid cross. Mendel’s first and second laws

blocks.text: A **monohybrid cross** is a cross of organisms that differ in one pair of alternative traits. When Mendel crossed yellow-seeded (AA) and green-seeded (aa) peas, all plants in F~1~ had yellow seeds (Aa); when F~1~ plants were crossed with each other, yellow and green seeds appeared in F~2~ in a 3 : 1 ratio (Figure 4.1).

blocks.label: Figure 4.1
blocks.caption: Mendel’s first and second laws shown in a Punnett square: crossing yellow (AA) and green (aa) peas, uniformity of F~1~ and segregation in F~2~ in a 3 : 1 ratio (P.Kh. Kholikov et al., 2022).

items: **Mendel’s first law (law of uniformity of first-generation hybrids):** when two homozygous organisms differing in alternative traits are crossed, F~1~ hybrids are uniform in genotype and phenotype.

**Mendel’s second law (law of segregation):** when F~1~ heterozygotes are crossed with each other, traits segregate in F~2~ in a 3 : 1 ratio by phenotype and 1 : 2 : 1 by genotype (1 AA : 2 Aa : 1 aa).

blocks.text: **Hypothesis of gamete purity:** in a hybrid organism allelic genes do not blend; each gamete receives **only one allele** of the pair. Its **cytological basis** is the separation of homologous chromosomes (and the alleles on them) into different gametes in anaphase I of meiosis.

A **test cross** is crossing an organism with a dominant phenotype with a recessive homozygote (aa) to determine its genotype. If all offspring show the dominant trait, the organism tested is homozygous (AA); if segregation in a 1 : 1 ratio occurs, it is heterozygous (Aa).

parts.text: Problem-solving algorithm: (1) denote the traits with letters; (2) write the genotypes of the parents; (3) determine the gametes of each (each gamete carries one allele of each gene); (4) draw the Punnett square; (5) calculate the genotype and phenotype ratio or the probability (%).

blocks.text: **Multiple allelism** is the presence of more than two alleles at one locus in a population, though each organism carries only two of them. In humans the **ABO blood groups** are determined by the alleles I^0^, I^A^ and I^B^: I^A^ and I^B^ are dominant over I^0^ and codominant with each other.

blocks.text: The **Rhesus factor** is determined by one main gene: Rh-positive (D — dominant) and Rh-negative (dd). If an Rh-negative mother carries an Rh-positive fetus, **Rh incompatibility** (hemolytic disease of the newborn) may develop in the second and later pregnancies.

parts.text: Blood group genetics is used in forensic medicine to **exclude** paternity: for example, a mother with group I (0) cannot have a child with group IV (AB). But blood groups **cannot prove** paternity — DNA analysis is needed for that. In the **Bombay phenomenon**, under the action of an epistatic recessive gene (hh), a person carrying the I^A^ or I^B^ gene appears to be group I (0).

sections.title: 4. Di- and polyhybrid crosses. Mendel’s third law

blocks.text: A **dihybrid cross** is a cross of organisms that differ in two pairs of alternative traits. When Mendel crossed yellow smooth (AABB) and green wrinkled (aabb) peas, all F~1~ were yellow smooth (AaBb). The F~1~ hybrid forms 4 kinds of gametes (AB, Ab, aB, ab), and in F~2~ there are 16 combinations, 9 genotypes and 4 phenotypes in a 9 : 3 : 3 : 1 ratio (Figure 4.2).

blocks.label: Figure 4.2
blocks.caption: Mendel’s third law (independent inheritance of traits) in a Punnett square: 16 combinations and the 9 : 3 : 3 : 1 phenotype ratio in the cross AaBb × AaBb; the letters under each genotype show the phenotype — D dominant, R recessive — for the first and second trait (P.Kh. Kholikov et al., 2022).

blocks.text: **Mendel’s third law (law of independent inheritance):** in a dihybrid cross, segregation for each pair of traits proceeds in a 3 : 1 ratio independently of the other pair, and genes combine in all possible combinations. The law holds only if the genes are located **on different pairs of chromosomes**. Its cytological basis is the independent separation of homologous pairs in metaphase I.
Independent assortment can be proved by a **test cross**: in the cross AaBb × aabb four phenotypes appear in a 1 : 1 : 1 : 1 ratio.

blocks.text: **Pleiotropy** is the effect of one gene on several traits. For example, in **Marfan syndrome** a mutation of the gene for the connective tissue protein fibrillin causes long “spider fingers”, dislocation of the lens and aortic aneurysm together; the **phenylketonuria** gene causes intellectual disability, light skin and hair and a peculiar odor of the urine.

parts.text: If the ratio adds up to **16**, a dihybrid cross (two genes) is involved: 9 + 7, 13 + 3, 12 + 3 + 1, 9 + 3 + 4, 15 + 1 are all “merged” variants of 9 : 3 : 3 : 1.

The expression of a gene is described by **penetrance** (the percentage of gene carriers in whom the trait appears) and **expressivity** (the degree to which the trait is expressed). For example, the polydactyly gene has incomplete penetrance.

cases.text: In humans curly hair (A) is dominant over straight hair (a). A heterozygous curly-haired man married a straight-haired woman.

cases.title: Case 2
cases.text: Wilson disease (disorder of copper metabolism) is inherited as an autosomal recessive trait. One parent is ill; the other is healthy and has healthy parents, but this parent’s brother has Wilson disease.
cases.ask: Determine the probability of an affected child in this family.
cases.answer: The affected parent is aa. The healthy parent comes from healthy parents who have an affected son, so their parents are Aa × Aa, and the healthy parent, being unaffected, is AA (1/3) or Aa (2/3). If he or she is Aa, the probability of an affected child in the marriage aa × Aa is 1/2. Overall probability: 2/3 × 1/2 = 1/3 (≈ 33 %). If the healthy partner is known to be heterozygous — 50 %, if homozygous — 0 %.

Children: AaBb (brown-eyed myopic), Aabb (brown-eyed normal), aaBb (blue-eyed myopic), aabb (blue-eyed normal) — each 1/4. The probability of a brown-eyed myopic child is 25 %.

topics.title: The chromosome theory of heredity. T.H. Morgan. Linked inheritance of genes, crossing over. Sex-linked inheritance of traits

goals.text: To teach the student T. Morgan’s chromosome theory of heredity, complete and incomplete linkage of genes, crossing over and the determination of distances between genes, genetic maps, the genetic determination of sex and the inheritance of X- and Y-linked traits.
By the end of the class the student should know:

items: the main statements of the chromosome theory of heredity;
the concepts of linkage group and complete and incomplete linkage;
the frequency of crossing over and the concept of the morganid;
the types of sex determination (XY, XO, ZW) and the genetic basis of sex development in humans;
the features of X-linked dominant and recessive and Y-linked (holandric) inheritance.

goals.text: The student should be able to:

items: solve problems on linked genes and calculate the distance between genes;
determine the order of three genes on a chromosome from the distances between them;
solve problems on sex-linked traits (color blindness, hemophilia).

blocks.text: Mendel’s third law holds only for genes on different chromosomes. The number of genes is much greater than the number of chromosomes (in humans there are about 20 thousand protein-coding genes on 46 chromosomes), so each chromosome carries many genes. The American geneticist **T.H. Morgan** and his students (A. Sturtevant, C. Bridges, H. Muller) carried out experiments on the fruit fly (*Drosophila melanogaster*) in 1910–1916 and created the **chromosome theory of heredity**.

parts.text: Drosophila is a convenient object for genetic research: it is easy to breed, one generation takes 10–12 days, it has many offspring, varied traits and few chromosomes (2n = 8).

blocks.text: Main statements of the chromosome theory

items: Genes are located on chromosomes; each chromosome carries particular genes.
Genes are arranged linearly on a chromosome in a definite order; each gene has its own locus.

Genes on one chromosome form a **linkage group** and are inherited together; the number of linkage groups equals the haploid number of chromosomes (in humans 23 in women and 24 in men — X and Y separately).
Genes are exchanged between homologous chromosomes by crossing over; its frequency is directly proportional to the distance between the genes.
The karyotype of each species is specific and constant.

blocks.text: Morgan crossed gray-bodied long-winged (BBVV) and black-bodied short-winged (bbvv) Drosophila and obtained gray long-winged flies (BbVv) in F~1~. When he then crossed an F~1~ male with a recessive female (bbvv) (a test cross), not the 1 : 1 : 1 : 1 expected by Mendel appeared, but only the two parental phenotypes in a 1 : 1 ratio (Figure 5.1). Hence the B and V genes lie on one chromosome and are inherited **completely linked**.

blocks.label: Figure 5.1
blocks.caption: Completely linked inheritance of the body color and wing length genes in Drosophila: B — gray body, b — black body, V — normal wings, v — short (vestigial) wings (P.Kh. Kholikov et al., 2022).

blocks.text: If an F~1~ **female** is used for the test cross, then besides the parental-type flies a small number (8.5 % each) of new combinations appear — gray short-winged and black long-winged (**crossover**, recombinant) flies: 41.5 % : 41.5 % : 8.5 % : 8.5 %. This is **incomplete linkage**, and its cause is crossing over during meiosis in the female Drosophila (there is no crossing over in the male Drosophila).

parts.text: Notation of linked genes: alleles on one chromosome are written on one side of the fraction line — **AB/ab** (cis position, dominant alleles on one chromosome) or **Ab/aB** (trans position, dominant alleles on different chromosomes).

blocks.text: **Crossing over** is the exchange of equal segments between chromatids of homologous chromosomes in prophase I of meiosis (pachytene) (Figure 5.2). It breaks linkage groups, creates new combinations of genes and is a source of combinative variability.

blocks.label: Figure 5.2
blocks.caption: Crossing over between homologous chromosomes: I — before crossing over; II — crossing over; III — recombinant chromatids after crossing over (P.Kh. Kholikov et al., 2022).

blocks.text: The **distance between genes** is measured by the frequency of crossing over: **1 % crossing over = 1 morganid (centimorgan, cM)**. The recombination frequency (rf) is calculated as follows:
rf (%) = (number of crossover individuals / total number of offspring) × 100

For example, in the experiment above crossover flies make up 8.5 % + 8.5 % = 17 %, so the distance between the B and V genes is 17 morganids. The greater the distance, the more crossing over occurs; but the frequency of crossing over does not exceed 50 % (at 50 % the genes appear to be inherited independently).

A **genetic map** is a diagram of the order of genes on a chromosome and the relative distances between them. Knowing the distances between three genes, their order can be determined: the largest distance lies between the outer genes and equals the sum of the other two distances (Figure 5.3).

blocks.label: Figure 5.3
blocks.caption: Constructing a gene map: 1.5 % crossing over between A and B, 3.5 % between B and C, 5.0 % between C and D; the distance A–D equals 10.0 % (numbers are the percentage of crossing over between genes) (P.Kh. Kholikov et al., 2022).

blocks.text: A complete map of the human genome has now been made: **genetic (recombination)** maps are built by studying crossing over in families, and **physical** maps by hybridization, FISH and DNA sequencing. They are used to find the genes of hereditary diseases and in prenatal diagnosis.

Sex is the set of traits that ensure the reproductive function of an organism; it is determined by the **sex chromosomes** (heterochromosomes). The other chromosomes are called **autosomes**. The human karyotype: in women 44 autosomes + XX (46,XX), in men 44 autosomes + XY (46,XY). The sex with identical sex chromosomes is **homogametic** (one kind of gamete), and the sex with different ones is **heterogametic**.

blocks.text: In humans sex is determined **at fertilization**: if an X-bearing sperm fertilizes the egg, a girl (XX) is born, and if a Y-bearing sperm does, a boy (XY); the theoretical ratio is 1 : 1. Male development is determined by the **SRY gene** on the Y chromosome (the testis-determining factor). That is why a person with the karyotype 47,XXY has a male phenotype and a person with 45,X a female phenotype.

parts.text: Disorders of sexual differentiation: 46,XX male syndrome when the SRY gene has moved to the X chromosome; female phenotype in a person with the 46,XY karyotype in androgen receptor deficiency (**testicular feminization syndrome**). In such cases the karyotype and sex chromatin are examined to determine sex.

blocks.text: Traits determined by genes located on the sex chromosomes are called **sex-linked** traits. In males the genes on the X chromosome are unpaired (**hemizygous**), so even a recessive allele is always expressed in a male.

blocks.text: In the example of **color blindness**: X^D^ — normal vision, X^d^ — color blindness. In a marriage of a carrier woman (X^D^X^d^) and a healthy man (X^D^Y), all daughters have normal vision (50 % of them carriers) and 50 % of the sons are color-blind. **Hemophilia** is inherited in the same way; its spread among the descendants of Queen Victoria of Great Britain is a famous example.

**Sex-limited (sex-influenced) traits** are determined by genes on autosomes but are expressed only in one sex or differently in the two sexes (under the influence of sex hormones): male-pattern baldness (androgenetic alopecia) — dominant in men and recessive in women; development of the mammary glands, beard growth, pitch of the voice.

parts.text: An X-linked recessive disease is **never passed from father to son**, because a son receives the Y chromosome from his father. The carrier of an affected son is always the mother.

cases.text: In humans the gene for color vision (D, dominant) and the gene for color blindness (d, recessive) are on the X chromosome. A color-blind daughter was born to a color-blind man and a woman with normal vision.
cases.ask: Determine the genotypes of the parents.
cases.answer: The color-blind daughter is X^d^X^d^ — she received one X^d^ from the father and the other from the mother. The father is color-blind — X^d^Y. The mother has normal vision but passed on X^d^, so she is a carrier — X^D^X^d^. In this family 50 % of both daughters and sons may be color-blind.

cases.title: Case 2
cases.text: Hypertrichosis (hair growth on the ear pinna) is Y-linked, and one form of ichthyosis is an X-linked recessive trait. A child with ichthyosis was born in the family of a woman healthy for both traits and a man with hypertrichosis.
cases.ask: Can this child have hypertrichosis? What is the child’s sex?
cases.answer: Ichthyosis is X-linked recessive; from healthy parents an affected child can only be a son (X^i^Y) who received X^i^ from a carrier mother (the father is X^I^Y, so his daughters cannot be affected). Since the child is a boy, he received the Y chromosome carrying the hypertrichosis gene from his father — he will have both ichthyosis and (at puberty) hypertrichosis.

cases.title: Case 3
cases.text: In humans cataract (A) and polydactyly (B) are determined by dominant genes completely linked on one autosome (no crossing over). The woman and the man are both diheterozygous; in each case the father had cataract and the mother had polydactyly.
cases.ask: What will be the genotypes and phenotypes of the children?
cases.answer: Each parent received the Ab chromosome from the father and aB from the mother, i.e., is a diheterozygote in the trans position Ab/aB. Without crossing over each forms only Ab and aB gametes. F~1~: Ab/Ab (cataract only) — 25 %, Ab/aB (cataract + polydactyly) — 50 %, aB/aB (polydactyly only) — 25 %. A healthy child (ab/ab) will not be born.

topics.title: Molecular basis of life. Nucleic acids and their role in passing hereditary traits from generation to generation. The role of DNA in protein biosynthesis. Genetic engineering. Variability and its forms

goals.text: To teach the student the evidence that DNA is the hereditary material, the structure and replication of nucleic acids, the properties of the genetic code, the stages of transcription and translation, the regulation of gene activity, the basics of gene and cell engineering, and the forms of variability and the classification of mutations.
By the end of the class the student should know:

items: the essence of the experiments on transformation, transduction and conjugation;
the structure of DNA and RNA, Chargaff’s rules and the semiconservative mode of replication;
the properties of the genetic code and the stages of protein biosynthesis;
the operon theory (induction and repression);
the types of variability, the classification of mutations, DNA repair and antimutagens.

goals.text: The student should be able to:

items: determine the complementary strand, mRNA and amino acid sequence from a DNA strand;
calculate the percentage of nucleotides using Chargaff’s rule;
identify the type of mutation from a description or a diagram.

sections.title: 1. Proof that DNA is the hereditary material

blocks.title: Table 6.1. Experiments that proved the role of DNA in heredity

Essence
Discoverers

F. Griffith (1928), O. Avery and colleagues (1944)

blocks.text: **Plasmids** are small circular DNA molecules in bacteria outside the chromosome; they replicate independently. The F plasmid ensures conjugation, and R plasmids provide **antibiotic resistance** and spread rapidly between bacteria. Plasmids are used as **vectors** in genetic engineering.

sections.title: 2. Structure of nucleic acids and DNA replication

blocks.text: Nucleic acids are biopolymers built of **nucleotides**. Each nucleotide consists of a nitrogenous base, a pentose (deoxyribose in DNA, ribose in RNA) and a phosphate residue. Nitrogenous bases: **purines** — adenine (A) and guanine (G); **pyrimidines** — cytosine (C), thymine (T, only in DNA) and uracil (U, only in RNA).

In 1953 **J. Watson and F. Crick** proposed the double helix model of DNA (based on the X-ray diffraction data of R. Franklin and M. Wilkins). DNA consists of two **antiparallel** (5′→3′ and 3′→5′) polynucleotide strands; the strands are joined by hydrogen bonds between nitrogenous bases according to the principle of **complementarity**: A=T (2 hydrogen bonds), G≡C (3 hydrogen bonds). The helix diameter is 2 nm, one turn contains 10 nucleotide pairs, the pitch is 3.4 nm and the distance between neighboring nucleotides is 0.34 nm (Figure 6.1).

blocks.label: Figure 6.1
blocks.caption: The twisted double-stranded DNA molecule: complementary base pairs and dimensions of the helix (diameter 2 nm, one turn 3.4 nm, distance between bases 0.34 nm) (P.Kh. Kholikov et al., 2022).

parts.text: **Chargaff’s rules:** A = T, G = C; the sum of purines equals the sum of pyrimidines (A + G = T + C). So if you know the percentage of one base in DNA, you can calculate the others: for example, if G = 20 %, then C = 20 % and A = T = 30 %.

blocks.title: Table 6.2. Differences between DNA and RNA
head: Feature
DNA
RNA
rows: mRNA (carries information), tRNA (carries amino acids), rRNA (part of ribosomes)

blocks.text: **Replication** is the self-duplication of DNA; it takes place in the S period of interphase. M. Meselson and F. Stahl (1958) proved that replication is **semiconservative**: each new DNA molecule has one old (template) strand and one new strand. In the process **helicase** unwinds the double helix, **topoisomerase** relieves the twisting, **primase** synthesizes an RNA primer and **DNA polymerase** builds the new strand only in the 5′→3′ direction; therefore one strand is made continuously (leading) and the other as Okazaki fragments (lagging), which are joined by **ligase**.

sections.title: 3. The genetic code and protein biosynthesis

blocks.text: The **genetic code** is the system of recording the amino acid sequence of a protein by the nucleotide sequence of mRNA. Its properties:

items: **Triplet** — each amino acid is coded by three nucleotides (a codon); there are 4^3^ = 64 codons, 61 of which code amino acids and 3 (UAA, UAG, UGA) are **stop codons**.
**Degeneracy (redundancy)** — most amino acids are coded by several codons (only methionine and tryptophan by one each).
**Unambiguity (specificity)** — each codon specifies only one amino acid.
**Continuity and non-overlapping** — there are no “commas” between codons, and one nucleotide does not belong to two codons.
**Universality** — the code is almost the same in all organisms.
**Start codon** — AUG (methionine).

blocks.title: Table 6.3. mRNA codons of some amino acids
head: Amino acid
Codons
Amino acid
Codons

UUA, UUG, CUU, CUC, CUA, CUG

blocks.text: **Transcription** is the synthesis of mRNA on one (template) strand of DNA by RNA polymerase (Figure 6.2). It starts at the promoter and ends at the terminator. In eukaryotes pre-mRNA is formed first; during **processing** a “cap” is added to the 5′ end and a poly-A “tail” to the 3′ end, and in **splicing** introns are cut out and exons are joined.

blocks.label: Figure 6.2
blocks.caption: Diagram of transcription: RNA polymerase opens the DNA double helix and synthesizes an RNA strand complementary to the template strand (P.Kh. Kholikov et al., 2022).

blocks.text: **Translation** is the synthesis of a polypeptide chain on the ribosome according to the information in mRNA (Figure 6.3). Amino acids are activated by special enzymes (aminoacyl-tRNA synthetases) and attached to tRNA. The **anticodon** of tRNA binds to the mRNA codon by complementarity.

items: **Initiation** — the small ribosomal subunit binds to mRNA, the tRNA carrying methionine takes its place at the start codon AUG, and then the large subunit joins.
**Elongation** — the next aminoacyl-tRNA arrives at the A site, a peptide bond forms between the amino acids, and the ribosome moves one codon (translocation).
**Termination** — when the ribosome reaches a stop codon, the polypeptide is released and the ribosome dissociates into subunits.

blocks.label: Figure 6.3
blocks.caption: Stages of protein biosynthesis (translation): initiation, elongation and termination; small and large ribosomal subunits, tRNA and mRNA (P.Kh. Kholikov et al., 2022).

parts.text: Many antibiotics stop bacterial translation: tetracyclines (binding of tRNA), streptomycin (the small subunit), chloramphenicol and macrolides (the large subunit). They act selectively on the 70S ribosomes of bacteria.

sections.title: 4. Regulation of gene activity and cytoplasmic heredity

blocks.text: F. Jacob and J. Monod (1961) created the **operon** theory in Escherichia coli. An operon is a group of structural genes transcribed together under one promoter and operator. A regulator gene synthesizes a **repressor** protein, which binds to the operator and blocks the movement of RNA polymerase.

items: **Induction** (lactose operon): without lactose in the medium the repressor is bound to the operator and the genes are off; lactose (the inducer) binds and inactivates the repressor — enzymes that break down lactose are synthesized.
**Repression** (tryptophan operon): when the end product (tryptophan) accumulates, it activates the repressor as a corepressor and synthesis stops.

blocks.text: In eukaryotes gene activity is regulated at many levels: chromatin condensation (DNA methylation, histone modification), transcription factors and enhancers, splicing, mRNA stability and translation.

**Cytoplasmic (extranuclear) heredity** is the inheritance of traits through the DNA of mitochondria and plastids. In humans mitochondria pass to the zygote only through the egg, so mitochondrial diseases (Leber hereditary optic neuropathy, MELAS) are passed **only from the mother** to all her children.
**Genetic engineering** is the set of methods for isolating desired genes, transferring them into the cells of another organism with a vector and using them. Its main stages:

items: Obtaining the desired gene — cutting DNA with **restriction enzymes** (for example, EcoRI) or synthesizing complementary DNA from mRNA with reverse transcriptase.
Joining the gene into a **vector** (plasmid, bacteriophage, virus) with **ligase** — forming recombinant DNA.
Introducing the recombinant DNA into a recipient cell (bacterium, yeast).
Selecting and multiplying (cloning) the cells that received the gene and isolating the product.

blocks.text: Genetic engineering is used to produce **human insulin**, growth hormone, interferons, hepatitis B vaccine and blood clotting factors; **gene therapy**, transgenic plants and animals, PCR (polymerase chain reaction) diagnosis and genome editing with CRISPR-Cas9 are developing.

**Cell engineering** is growing cells, hybridizing them (somatic hybridization) and cloning by nuclear transfer. **Hybridomas** obtained by fusing a lymphocyte with a tumor cell produce monoclonal antibodies. The sheep “Dolly” was cloned by nuclear transfer in 1996.

blocks.text: By the site of origin, **somatic** mutations (in body cells — not inherited, cause tumors and mosaicism) and **generative** mutations (in sex cells — passed to offspring) are distinguished. By cause, there are **spontaneous** (natural, cause unknown) and **induced** (under the action of mutagens) mutations. Mutagens: **physical** (ionizing and ultraviolet radiation, high temperature), **chemical** (alkylating agents, nitrous acid, benzopyrene, some drugs), **biological** (viruses, mobile genetic elements).

**DNA repair** is the system that restores damaged DNA: **photoreactivation** (splitting thymine dimers in light), **excision repair** (cutting out the damaged segment and rebuilding it with DNA polymerase and ligase) and **postreplicative repair**. If repair fails, mutations accumulate: for example, in **xeroderma pigmentosum** ultraviolet light causes skin cancer. **Antimutagens** are substances that reduce the frequency of mutations: vitamins (A, E, C), selenium, some amino acids, antioxidants.

parts.text: **Sickle cell anemia** is a classic point mutation: the substitution GAG → GTG in codon 6 of the β-globin gene puts valine in place of glutamic acid (HbS). At low oxygen HbS polymerizes, the erythrocyte takes a sickle shape and blocks the capillaries.

topics.title: Methods of studying human genetics: the genealogical, twin and population-statistical methods

goals.text: To teach the student the specific features of studying humans as a genetic object, the rules of drawing a pedigree and the criteria for determining the type of inheritance by the genealogical method, the assessment of the role of heredity and environment by the twin method, and the population-statistical method and the Hardy-Weinberg law.
By the end of the class the student should know:

items: the difficulties of studying human genetics and the system of methods;
the terms and symbols used in drawing a pedigree;
the criteria of autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive and sex-linked inheritance;
monozygotic and dizygotic twins, concordance and Holzinger’s formula;
the concepts of population, deme and isolate and the Hardy-Weinberg law.

goals.text: The student should be able to:

items: draw and analyze a pedigree of one’s own family and from the conditions of a problem;
determine the type of inheritance and assess the risk for the next children;
calculate allele and genotype frequencies by the Hardy-Weinberg formula.

blocks.text: Human genetics obeys the laws of heredity common to all living organisms, but the classical hybridization method cannot be used to study humans. The reasons are:

items: experimental (purposeful) crossing is impossible in humans;
generations change slowly (25–30 years) and the number of children is small;
the karyotype is complex (46 chromosomes) and there are many linkage groups;
humans cannot be kept and observed under identical environmental conditions;
there are medical and ethical restrictions.

blocks.text: Therefore special methods are used in human genetics: the **genealogical, twin, population-statistical, cytogenetic, dermatoglyphic, biochemical, molecular genetic and immunogenetic** methods, somatic cell genetics and modeling. Human genetics also has advantages: the human phenotype and diseases are studied more deeply than in other organisms, populations are large, and written records exist for many generations.

The **genealogical method** (F. Galton, 1865) determines whether a trait is hereditary, its type of inheritance and the genotypes of family members by drawing and analyzing a pedigree. The method has two stages: collecting information and drawing the pedigree; genetic analysis of the pedigree.

blocks.text: The classic example of a hemophilia pedigree is the family of **Queen Victoria** of Great Britain (Figure 7.3). Victoria was a carrier of the hemophilia gene; her son Leopold was affected and her daughters Alice and Beatrice were carriers, and the gene spread to the royal families of Germany, Russia and Spain (the Russian heir to the throne Alexei also had hemophilia).

blocks.text: The **twin method** (F. Galton, 1876) compares traits in monozygotic and dizygotic twins to determine the relative role of heredity and environment in their formation. Twins are born in about 1 % of human births.

blocks.text: The presence of a trait in both twins is called **concordance**, and its presence in only one is called **discordance**. The percentage of concordance is compared in MZ and DZ pairs: if concordance in MZ is much higher than in DZ, heredity plays an important role in the development of the trait. The **coefficient of heritability** is calculated by Holzinger’s formula:
Here C is the percentage of concordance, H the share of heredity and E the share of environment. If H > 0.7, the trait is determined mainly by heredity; if H < 0.4, mainly by the environment.

parts.text: In measles concordance is almost equally high in MZ and DZ — susceptibility to this disease depends mainly on the environment (contact with the virus). In schizophrenia and type 2 diabetes MZ concordance is much higher — these are **diseases with a hereditary predisposition (multifactorial)**.

blocks.text: A **population** is a group of individuals of one species living for a long time in a certain area and freely marrying each other. In humans small groups are distinguished within large populations: a **deme** (1500–4000 people, marriages within the group 80–90 %) and an **isolate** (up to 1500 people, marriages within the group more than 90 %). In isolates consanguineous marriages are common, so the frequency of recessive diseases rises (geographic, religious, ethnic isolates).

In a population of self-fertilizing organisms the proportion of heterozygotes halves in each generation and the population splits into homozygous lines. In cross-fertilizing (panmictic) populations the ratio of genotypes obeys the **Hardy-Weinberg law**:

Here p is the frequency of the dominant allele (A), q the frequency of the recessive allele (a), and p^2^, 2pq and q^2^ the frequencies of the genotypes AA, Aa and aa. The law holds for an **ideal population**: the population is large, mating is random (panmixia), and there are no mutations, natural selection or migration.

parts.text: Calculation always starts from the **recessive homozygotes**, because only their phenotype matches their genotype: for example, if phenylketonuria occurs at 1 : 10000, then q^2^ = 0.0001, q = 0.01 and p = 0.99; heterozygous carriers 2pq ≈ 0.02, i.e., one in every 50 people.

blocks.text: **Stages of the population-statistical method:** choosing the population, collecting data (frequency of the disease or trait), statistical analysis. The method is used to determine allele and genotype frequencies, the spread of hereditary diseases and carriers and their geographic and ethnic differences, the frequency of mutations, and to plan medical genetic services.

goals.text: To teach the student the methods of analyzing the human karyotype, the classification of chromosomes (Denver and Paris nomenclatures), the detection of sex chromatin and its medical importance, the basics of dermatoglyphic analysis, biochemical, molecular genetic and immunogenetic methods, and the methods of prenatal diagnosis.
By the end of the class the student should know:

the Denver groups of chromosomes (A–G);
sex X chromatin (the Barr body) and “drumsticks”, and the Lyon hypothesis;
the types of finger and palm patterns, the atd angle and dermatoglyphic changes in diseases;

goals.text: The student should be able to:

sections.title: 1. The cytogenetic method and karyotype analysis

blocks.text: The **cytogenetic method** is the microscopic study of the number and structure of chromosomes. The number of human chromosomes was established precisely in 1956 by J. Tjio and A. Levan (2n = 46). **Peripheral blood lymphocytes** are most often used for the test, as well as bone marrow, skin fibroblasts, amniocytes and chorionic cells.

items: Lymphocytes are cultured in a nutrient medium for 72 hours under the action of **phytohemagglutinin** (a mitogen).
Division is arrested in metaphase with **colchicine**.
The cells are treated with a **hypotonic solution** (0.075 M KCl) — they swell and the chromosomes spread out.
Fixation (methanol + acetic acid), dropping onto a slide and staining.
Metaphase plates are studied under the microscope and photographed, and a **karyogram** (chromosomes arranged in pairs) is made.

blocks.text: **Staining methods:** routine staining allows chromosomes to be grouped only by size and shape; **differential staining** (G-, Q-, R- and C-banding) produces a specific pattern of transverse bands on each chromosome and makes it possible to identify each pair and small aberrations (Figure 8.1). Modern methods are **FISH** (fluorescence in situ hybridization) and chromosomal microarray analysis.

blocks.caption: Diagram of differentially stained human chromosomes (idiogram): 22 pairs of autosomes and the sex chromosomes (X, Y); the outlined pairs — 13, 18, 21 — are those most often involved in chromosomal diseases (P.Kh. Kholikov et al., 2022).

Pairs

blocks.text: **Karyotype notation (ISCN):** first the total number of chromosomes, then the sex chromosomes, then the anomaly: 46,XX — normal female; 46,XY — normal male; 47,XY,+21 — male with Down syndrome; 46,XX,5p^−^ — deletion of the short arm of chromosome 5; 46,XY/47,XY,+21 — mosaicism. Chromosome arms: p — short, q — long.

parts.text: An **idiogram** is a schematic drawing of chromosomes with their differentially stained bands. A **karyogram** is a picture of the chromosomes of a metaphase plate of a particular person arranged in pairs.

blocks.text: **Sex X chromatin (the Barr body)** is a small (≈ 1 µm), densely staining triangular or crescent-shaped body lying under the nuclear envelope in the interphase nucleus. It was discovered in 1949 by M. Barr and E. Bertram in cat neurons. The Barr body is an **inactivated X chromosome**.

**The Lyon hypothesis** (M. Lyon, 1961): in the somatic cells of a woman, at an early stage of embryonic development (about day 16), one of the X chromosomes is randomly inactivated and becomes heterochromatin. Because of this the female body is a **mosaic** of cells with an active paternal or maternal X chromosome; this equalizes the dosage of genes in males and females (**dosage compensation**).

parts.text: **Number of Barr bodies = number of X chromosomes − 1.** 46,XY and 45,X — 0; 46,XX and 47,XXY — 1; 47,XXX and 48,XXXY — 2.

blocks.text: Sex chromatin is detected in the epithelium of the oral mucosa (buccal smear) and vaginal epithelium: the smear is stained with aceto-orcein or hematoxylin and 100 nuclei are counted. In a normal woman X chromatin is found in 20–40 % of nuclei, in a man in 0–2 %. In neutrophil leukocytes X chromatin appears as a **“drumstick”** projecting from the segmented nucleus (in 1–5 % of neutrophils in women) (Figure 8.2). **Y chromatin** is detected in male cells stained with quinacrine as a bright dot under the fluorescence microscope.

blocks.text: **Dermatoglyphics** is the study of the papillary ridges (patterns) on the skin of the fingers, palms and soles. The patterns form in months 3–6 of fetal life and do not change throughout life; they are inherited **polygenically**. **Dactyloscopy** studies finger patterns, **palmoscopy** palm patterns and **plantoscopy** sole patterns.

sections.title: 4. Biochemical, molecular genetic and immunogenetic methods

blocks.text: The **biochemical method** detects hereditary disorders of metabolism (enzymopathies). It is carried out in two stages: (1) **screening (rapid)** — testing many people with simple qualitative reactions (for example, a green color when FeCl~3~ is added to urine in phenylketonuria; measuring phenylalanine and TSH in a drop of heel blood in newborns); (2) **confirmatory** — quantitative measurement of metabolites and enzyme activity in blood, urine and tissues (chromatography, electrophoresis, tandem mass spectrometry).

**Molecular genetic methods** analyze at the DNA level: isolating DNA and RNA from biological material (blood, buccal epithelium, chorion, amniocytes), **PCR** (polymerase chain reaction — copying a desired DNA segment millions of times), cutting with restriction enzymes and gel electrophoresis, **sequencing** (reading the nucleotide sequence), hybridization with DNA probes and FISH. They are used to detect gene mutations and carriers, for prenatal diagnosis and to establish paternity.

The **immunogenetic method** studies the polymorphism of blood groups, erythrocyte and leukocyte antigens (the HLA system) and serum proteins by antigen-antibody reactions. It is used to select donors in transplantation, to prevent Rh incompatibility, to establish paternity and to assess predisposition to diseases. **Monoclonal antibodies** are identical antibodies obtained from a single cell clone (a hybridoma) and directed against one antigenic determinant; **polyclonal** antibodies come from different clones and are directed against several determinants of the antigen.

**Prenatal diagnosis** is the detection of hereditary diseases and developmental defects in the fetus before birth. Its tasks are to prevent the birth of a child with a severe hereditary pathology, to plan pregnancy and delivery correctly and to start early treatment of some diseases.

cases.title: Case 1
cases.text: When the cells of a newborn with a female phenotype were examined cytogenetically, the karyogram showed 44 autosomes and the X and Y chromosomes.
cases.ask: What is the doctor’s conclusion?
cases.answer: The karyotype is 46,XY — genetically male, while the phenotype is female. This is a disorder of sexual differentiation: most often a mutation of the androgen receptor gene (testicular feminization syndrome — the testes lie in the abdomen or the inguinal canal) or loss/mutation of the SRY gene (Swyer syndrome). No X chromatin is found in a buccal smear. Hormonal and molecular tests and consultation with an endocrinologist and a geneticist are needed.

cases.title: Case 2
cases.text: The karyogram of a child referred for genetic counseling showed trisomy for one of the chromosomes of group D (pairs 13–15).
cases.ask: What is the doctor’s conclusion, and how can the exact pair be determined?
cases.answer: Group D trisomy most often concerns pair 13 (Patau syndrome, 47,XX(XY),+13): microcephaly, cleft lip and palate, polydactyly, heart defects, microphthalmia. With routine staining chromosomes 13, 14 and 15 cannot be told apart, so the exact pair must be determined by differential (G-) banding or FISH.

cases.title: Case 3
cases.text: Buccal smears were examined in patients with the karyotypes 47,XXY; 48,XXYY; 48,XXXY.
cases.ask: How many Barr bodies will there be in each case? Prove your answer.
cases.answer: The number of Barr bodies is one less than the number of X chromosomes (the Lyon rule: all X chromosomes except one are inactivated). 47,XXY — 1; 48,XXYY — 1; 48,XXXY — 2. The number of Y chromosomes does not affect the number of Barr bodies. All are variants of Klinefelter syndrome; intellectual disability becomes more severe as the number of X chromosomes increases.

blocks.text: **Hereditary diseases** are diseases caused by changes in the hereditary apparatus (gene, chromosome, genome) that can be passed on to the next generations. They may be congenital or may appear later (for example, Huntington disease at the age of 35–45). A **congenital disease** is not always hereditary: congenital defects also arise from intrauterine infection or teratogens.

blocks.text: **Syndromes caused by changes in chromosome structure:** **cri-du-chat** syndrome (46,5p^−^ — deletion of the short arm of chromosome 5): the infant’s cry resembles a cat’s mewing (underdeveloped larynx), microcephaly, moon face, hypertelorism, severe intellectual disability. **18q^−^ syndrome** (deletion of the long arm of chromosome 18): intellectual disability, microcephaly, facial and ear anomalies. **Wolf-Hirschhorn** (4p^−^), **Williams** (7q11.23 microdeletion) and **DiGeorge** (22q11.2 microdeletion) syndromes also belong to this group.

parts.text: Common signs of chromosomal diseases: **multiple congenital defects**, delay of intellectual and physical development, a dysmorphic face (minor anomalies) and altered dermatoglyphics. The diagnosis is confirmed only by **karyotyping**. Most of them arise anew (de novo) and are not passed on, because patients are often infertile.

blocks.text: Most gene diseases are **enzymopathies**: as a result of a mutation an enzyme is not synthesized or its activity decreases, the preceding metabolites accumulate and have a toxic effect, while the next product is deficient. They are mostly inherited as autosomal recessive.

sections.title: 5. Diseases with hereditary predisposition. Genocopy and phenocopy

blocks.text: **Diseases with hereditary predisposition (multifactorial)** are produced by the sum of the small effects of several genes (a polygenic system) together with environmental factors. They are the most common (hypertension, atherosclerosis, type 2 diabetes, bronchial asthma, peptic ulcer, schizophrenia, psoriasis, many congenital defects). Typical features: clustering of the disease in families, but not in Mendelian ratios; the risk rises with closer kinship and with more affected persons in the family; prevention is possible by changing environmental factors (diet, smoking, stress).

blocks.text: **Outbreeding** is marriage between unrelated persons; it reduces the probability that recessive alleles become homozygous and increases heterozygosity in the population. **Inbreeding** is marriage between relatives. Relatives may have received the same recessive alleles from a common ancestor, so such marriages increase the frequency of autosomal recessive diseases, congenital defects, stillbirths and miscarriages.

parts.text: In a marriage of first cousins the risk of a child with severe hereditary pathology is about 2 times higher (≈ 5–6 %) than the risk in the general population (≈ 3 %); if there is a recessive disease in the family, the risk is even higher. Such couples should definitely undergo genetic counseling.

blocks.text: **Medical genetic counseling** is specialized medical care aimed at preventing the birth of children with hereditary pathology. Its aim is to determine and explain the level of genetic risk to the family and to help it make a decision about having children. Counseling is **prospective** (before marriage or pregnancy, before an affected child is born) or **retrospective** (after an affected child has been born in the family).
Indications for referral to MGC

items: a child with a hereditary disease or congenital defect in the family;
consanguineous marriage;
maternal age over 35;
recurrent miscarriage, stillbirth, infertility;
exposure to teratogenic factors (drugs, radiation, infections) during pregnancy;
high risk in prenatal screening.

**Conclusion and explanation** — the risk, the severity of the disease and the possibilities of treatment and prenatal diagnosis are explained to the family in plain words; the decision is made by the family.

cases.title: Case 1
cases.text: When the patient’s karyotype was examined, some cells were found to be 45,X and others 46,XX.
cases.ask: How can this be explained?
cases.answer: This is mosaicism — 45,X/46,XX (the mosaic form of Shereshevsky-Turner syndrome). The zygote was normal (46,XX), but in one of the early cleavage divisions an X chromosome was lost (anaphase lag) or failed to separate, giving rise to two cell lines. The signs are usually milder than in the complete form of the syndrome, and some patients may be fertile.

cases.title: Case 2
cases.text: A marriage of first cousins produced 2 children: one had developmental defects, the other severe intellectual disability.
cases.ask: Explain the cause genetically.
cases.answer: First cousins share 1/8 of their genes, and the inbreeding coefficient of their children is 1/16: there is a high probability that both parents carry the same recessive allele from the common grandparents. As a result the children become homozygous (aa) for that allele and autosomal recessive diseases appear (for example, enzymopathies with intellectual disability such as phenylketonuria, or syndromes of congenital defects). Genetic counseling, clarification of the diagnosis and prenatal diagnosis are recommended before the next pregnancy.

cases.title: Case 3
cases.text: A child with a hereditary disease was born in a family that had undergone genetic counseling and in which an affected child was not expected.
cases.ask: How can this be explained?
cases.answer: Possible reasons: (1) a new (de novo) mutation or chromosomal error arose in a sex cell of one parent — such cases cannot be predicted in advance; (2) low risk does not mean zero risk — the probability was realized; (3) the disease was hidden in the family because of incomplete penetrance or genocopy; (4) germline mosaicism; (5) uncertain paternity or an incorrect diagnosis. The diagnosis of the new child must be clarified and the risk recalculated.

blocks.text: **Ontogenesis** (E. Haeckel, 1866) is the individual development of an organism: the set of changes from the formation of the zygote (in asexual reproduction — from separation from the parent) until death. It is **direct** (without a larva — reptiles, birds, mammals) or **indirect** (with metamorphosis — amphibians, insects). Direct development is in turn divided into the **egg-laying** and **intrauterine** types; the intrauterine type is characteristic of humans.
