blocks.text: **Gametogenesis** is the formation of gametes in the gonads. **Spermatogenesis** proceeds in four stages in the seminiferous tubules of the testis, and **oogenesis** in three stages in the ovary (Figure 10.1).

blocks.text: The **spermatozoon** is a motile cell consisting of a head (the nucleus and, in front of it, the enzyme-rich **acrosome**), a neck (centrioles), a middle piece (spirally arranged mitochondria — energy for movement) and a tail (axoneme, 9 + 2). A human spermatozoon is ≈ 60 µm long. The **egg** is immotile and large (≈ 130–150 µm in humans), with nutrients (yolk) in its cytoplasm; it is surrounded by a transparent coat (zona pellucida) and the **corona radiata** made of follicular cells.

parts.text: In oogenesis, **dictyotene** is the arrest of primary oocytes in diplotene of meiosis I from birth until ovulation (12–50 years). Meiosis I is completed before ovulation, and meiosis II is completed only when a spermatozoon enters the egg.

blocks.text: **Fertilization** is the fusion of a spermatozoon and an egg forming a diploid **zygote**; in humans it takes place in the ampulla of the uterine tube. Stages: approach of spermatozoa to the egg and the **acrosome reaction** (enzymes dissolve the corona radiata and zona pellucida), entry of one spermatozoon, the **cortical reaction** (blocking entry of other spermatozoa — prevention of polyspermy), and fusion of the male and female pronuclei (syngamy).

**Cleavage** is a series of mitotic divisions of the zygote; the cells formed (**blastomeres**) do not grow and become smaller with each division. The type of cleavage depends on the amount of yolk: **complete (holoblastic)** — equal (lancelet) or unequal (amphibians; asynchronous in humans); **incomplete (meroblastic)** — discoidal (birds, reptiles) or superficial (insects) (Figure 10.2). Cleavage gives a **morula** and then a hollow **blastula**; in mammals it is called a **blastocyst** (trophoblast + embryoblast) and is **implanted** in the uterine wall on day 7.

blocks.label: Figure 10.2
blocks.caption: Types of cleavage: 1 — radial (lancelet, mammals); 2 — spiral (flatworms and annelids, mollusks); 3 — bilateral (ascarids); 4 — anarchic; on the right — holoblastic, discoidal and superficial cleavage (P.Kh. Kholikov et al., 2022).

blocks.text: **Gastrulation** is the formation of a two- and then three-layered embryo — the **gastrula** — from the single-layered blastula; the **germ layers** — **ectoderm**, **endoderm** and **mesoderm** — are formed (Figure 10.3). Methods: **invagination** (infolding — lancelet), **immigration** (migration of cells inward), **delamination** (splitting into layers) and **epiboly** (overgrowth — amphibians). Then **neurulation** (formation of the neural tube and notochord) and **histo-organogenesis** begin.

sections.title: 4. Mechanisms of ontogenesis, critical periods and teratogenic factors

blocks.text: In ontogenesis cells **divide, migrate, differentiate** and **die** (apoptosis). Early blastomeres are **totipotent** — each can give rise to a whole organism (identical twins arise on this basis). **Differentiation** is the structural and functional specialization of cells with the same genotype as a result of activation of different genes. **Embryonic induction** (H. Spemann, 1924) is the determination of the developmental fate of one part of the embryo by another part (the inducer, for example chordamesoderm) (formation of the neural tube from ectoderm).

**Critical periods** are the periods when the embryo is most sensitive to harmful factors (P.G. Svetlov): the period of **implantation** (weeks 1–2 — harmful effects follow the “all or nothing” principle: the embryo dies or recovers completely) and the period of **organogenesis** (weeks 3–8 — severe congenital defects), as well as the period of **placentation**. In the fetal period harmful effects mainly cause functional disorders and growth retardation.

parts.text: When planning a pregnancy, taking **folic acid** (3 months before pregnancy and in the first trimester) markedly reduces the risk of neural tube defects; alcohol, smoking and taking drugs without a doctor’s advice are forbidden in pregnancy, and vaccination against rubella is given before pregnancy.

blocks.text: In postnatal development the organism grows, organs mature and puberty occurs. Growth and development are controlled by the **genotype**, **hormones** (growth hormone, thyroxine, sex hormones, insulin) and **environmental** factors (nutrition, physical activity, social conditions). The biological age of the organism is assessed by the skeleton, teeth, sexual maturation and other indicators and may differ from the chronological age (acceleration and retardation).

**Aging** is a natural process in which the adaptive capacity of the organism gradually decreases and the probability of disease and death increases. Aging and old age are studied by **gerontology**, and the diseases of the elderly and their treatment by **geriatrics**.

blocks.title: Table 10.6. Main theories of aging
head: Theory

rows: Human fibroblasts divide only ≈ 50 times in culture; telomeres shorten with each division
Reactive oxygen species damage DNA, proteins and membranes; the damage accumulates

blocks.text: **Progeria** is a hereditary disease with premature aging: Hutchinson-Gilford progeria in children (mutation of the lamin A gene) and Werner syndrome in adults (a DNA helicase gene). **Death** is the cessation of the vital activity of the organism: **clinical death** (breathing and heart activity have stopped, but recovery by resuscitation is possible within 5–6 minutes) and **biological death** (irreversible changes, first of all in the cerebral cortex).

**Regeneration** is the restoration of lost or damaged parts of the organism. **Physiological regeneration** is the renewal of worn-out cells in the normal course of life (epidermis, intestinal epithelium, blood cells). **Reparative regeneration** is restoration after injury: **complete** (restitution — the original tissue is restored) and **incomplete** (substitution — a scar forms). Methods: epimorphosis (growth from the wound surface), morphallaxis (rebuilding of the remaining part), regenerative hypertrophy (in the liver and kidney — the volume of the organ is restored, but not its shape). The capacity for regeneration decreases in the course of evolution and with age.

head: Type

rows: The same organism (from oneself to oneself — skin, bone)

blocks.text: Graft rejection is the response of the recipient’s immune system to the donor’s foreign **HLA antigens** (histocompatibility antigens, on chromosome 6). To prevent rejection, the donor is selected by HLA and immunosuppressants are used. Avascular tissues such as the cornea and cartilage are rarely rejected.

**Homeostasis** (W. Cannon, 1929) is the ability of the organism to keep its internal environment (temperature, pH, osmotic pressure, glucose and ion levels) relatively constant. It is maintained at the **genetic** (stability of genotype and karyotype — DNA repair), **structural** (preservation of the composition of cells and tissues — regeneration) and **physiological** levels by the nervous, endocrine and immune systems on the principle of **feedback**.

cases.title: Case 1
cases.text: In humans 4 spermatozoa are formed from one spermatogonium during spermatogenesis.
cases.ask: How many stages does spermatogenesis have? At which stage are spermatozoa formed? What are their chromosome set and DNA content?
cases.answer: Spermatogenesis has 4 stages: multiplication (spermatogonia, 2n2c), growth (primary spermatocyte, 2n4c), maturation (meiosis I — secondary spermatocytes n2c, meiosis II — spermatids 1n1c) and formation (spermiogenesis — spermatozoa from spermatids). Spermatozoa are formed at the formation stage; they are haploid — 1n1c (in humans 23 chromosomes: 22 autosomes + X or Y).

cases.title: Case 2
cases.text: In human oogenesis one egg is formed from one oogonium at the maturation stage.
cases.ask: What stages does oogenesis have? What other cells are formed at the maturation stage, and what process is this stage related to?
cases.answer: Oogenesis has 3 stages: multiplication (completed in fetal life), growth and maturation. In maturation, meiosis I gives a secondary oocyte and the first polar body, and meiosis II gives the egg and the second polar body; in total 1 egg and 3 polar bodies (the cytoplasm is divided unequally and nutrients accumulate in the egg). Maturation is related to monthly ovulation after puberty: meiosis I is completed before ovulation, and meiosis II at fertilization.

cases.title: Case 3
cases.text: In week 5 of pregnancy a woman took a drug for a long time without medical supervision, and later heart and limb defects were found in the fetus. Another woman took the same drug in week 30 of pregnancy, but no defects were found.
cases.ask: Explain the difference in the results.
cases.answer: Week 5 falls in the critical period of organogenesis (weeks 3–8): in this period the organ primordia are formed, and a teratogenic effect leads to severe anatomical defects. By week 30 the organs are already formed (fetal period), so a teratogenic effect may cause mainly functional disorders and growth retardation rather than major defects. The consequence of a teratogenic effect depends on the type of substance, its dose and the stage of pregnancy.

blocks.text: **Parasitism** is a form of relationship in which one organism (the parasite) uses another (the host) as its habitat and source of food and harms it. **Medical parasitology** studies protozoa (**protozoology**), helminths (**helminthology**) and arthropods (**arachnoentomology**) that parasitize humans.

blocks.text: Parasites enter humans by the **oral** (alimentary), **airborne**, **contact** (skin, sexual), **vector-borne** (arthropod bites) and **transplacental** routes. They harm the host by **mechanical** action (tissue damage, blocking ducts), **toxic-allergic** action, **taking nutrients** and **opening the way to secondary infection**.

sections.title: 2. The phylum Protozoa. Flagellates — human parasites

blocks.text: **Protozoa** are eukaryotes consisting of a single cell that performs all vital functions as an independent organism. Organelles of movement: pseudopodia (sarcodines), flagella (flagellates), cilia (ciliates); sporozoa have no special organelles of movement. Under unfavorable conditions most of them form a **cyst** — this is important for their spread.

Members of the **class Flagellata** have one or more flagella, often an **undulating membrane** and a **kinetoplast** (a mass of mitochondrial DNA at the base of the flagellum); they reproduce by longitudinal binary fission.

blocks.text: The trophozoite of **Giardia** is pear-shaped, 10–18 µm long and bilaterally symmetrical: it has two nuclei, four pairs of flagella and a ventral **sucking disc**; with the disc it attaches to the intestinal epithelium and impairs absorption (Figure 11.2). Its cysts are oval, with 4 nuclei, and resistant in the environment.

parts.text: In Uzbekistan **cutaneous leishmaniasis** (oriental sore) forms natural foci in desert and semi-desert areas near gerbil burrows. A papule appears at the bite site and turns into a long-lasting ulcer that heals with a scar. Prevention: protection from sandflies (nets, repellents), control of rodents, vaccination.

blocks.text: All members of the **class Sporozoa** are obligate parasites; they have no organelles of movement, and at the anterior end there is an **apical complex** for entering the host cell. Their life cycle alternates asexual reproduction (**schizogony**), sexual reproduction (**gametogony**) and **sporogony**.
**Malaria plasmodia** belong to the genus *Plasmodium*; the definitive host and specific vector is the female **Anopheles** mosquito, and the intermediate host is the human (Figure 11.3).

items: When the mosquito bites, **sporozoites** enter the blood with its saliva and within 30 minutes enter liver cells.

**Tissue (pre-erythrocytic) schizogony** — multiplication in the liver cell produces thousands of **merozoites** (incubation period). In *P. vivax* and *P. ovale* some sporozoites become dormant **hypnozoites** — the cause of late relapses of the disease.

**Erythrocytic schizogony** — merozoites enter erythrocytes: ring trophozoite → amoeboid trophozoite → schizont → morula (8–24 merozoites). When the erythrocytes burst and merozoites enter the blood, a **malaria paroxysm** (chills, fever, sweating) occurs.
Some merozoites give rise to male and female **gametocytes**; they pass with blood into the mosquito.

In the mosquito’s stomach **gametogony** (fertilization → motile zygote — ookinete → oocyst) and **sporogony** (thousands of sporozoites in the oocyst) take place; sporozoites gather in the salivary glands.

blocks.caption: Life cycle of *Plasmodium falciparum*: the process in the Anopheles mosquito (gametogony and sporogony) and in the human body (tissue schizogony in the liver, erythrocytic schizogony in the blood, formation of gametocytes) (P.Kh. Kholikov et al., 2022).

parts.text: Diagnosis — a **thick drop** and a **thin smear** taken during a paroxysm are stained by the Romanowsky-Giemsa method and examined; rapid antigen tests are also used. **Tropical malaria** is the most dangerous: infected erythrocytes stick to capillaries, causing cerebral malaria and death. Every person with fever returning from a malaria area must be tested immediately. Uzbekistan was certified malaria-free by the WHO in 2018.

blocks.text: **Toxoplasma** (*Toxoplasma gondii*) is an intracellular parasite shaped like a crescent or an orange segment, 4–7 µm long and 2–4 µm wide. **The definitive host is the cat** (sexual reproduction in its intestine, oocysts in feces); the **intermediate hosts** are humans and many mammals and birds (cysts in tissues). It enters humans through hands, vegetables and water contaminated with oocysts, through undercooked meat containing cysts and by the **transplacental** route. Primary infection in pregnancy causes fetal death, hydrocephalus, chorioretinitis and calcifications in the brain; in immunodeficiency (AIDS) it causes severe encephalitis. Diagnosis — serology (IgM, IgG), PCR.
**Coccidia** (*Isospora*, *Cryptosporidium*) parasitize the intestinal epithelium and cause diarrhea; cryptosporidiosis is severe in patients with AIDS.

sections.title: 4. Intestinal parasites: the dysentery amoeba and balantidium

blocks.text: The **dysentery amoeba** (*Entamoeba histolytica*, class Sarcodina) is the agent of **amoebiasis**; it is widespread in tropical and subtropical countries, including Central Asia. It lives in the large intestine and occurs in several forms (Figure 11.5):

items: **small vegetative (luminal) form** — 15–20 µm, feeds on bacteria and does not cause disease (carrier state);
**large vegetative, tissue and erythrophagous form** — 30–40 µm, invades the intestinal wall, forms ulcers and **ingests erythrocytes** (the main diagnostic sign);
**cyst** — 10–15 µm, with 4 nuclei, the invasive form; survives for a long time in the environment.

blocks.label: Figure 11.5
blocks.caption: Various forms of the dysentery amoeba: tissue form, small vegetative form, cyst and the hematophagous (erythrophagous) form with ingested erythrocytes (P.Kh. Kholikov et al., 2022).

blocks.text: Humans swallow cysts with contaminated water, unwashed fruit and vegetables, hands and flies. Amoebiasis causes **diarrhea with blood and mucus** (“raspberry jelly”), abdominal pain and ulcers in the large intestine; complications are intestinal perforation and **liver abscess**. Diagnosis — tissue forms with ingested erythrocytes in a wet smear of fresh stool (within 15–20 minutes), cysts in remission; endoscopy, serology.

**Intestinal balantidium** (*Balantidium coli*, class Ciliata) is the only ciliate that parasitizes humans and the largest protozoan (50–80 µm). Its body is covered with cilia; it has a large (macronucleus) and a small (micronucleus) nucleus, a mouth opening (cytostome) and contractile vacuoles. **The main reservoir is the pig**; pig farm workers are affected more often. It forms ulcers in the wall of the large intestine and causes **balantidiasis** with bloody-purulent diarrhea. Diagnosis — motile trophozoites and cysts in stool.

parts.text: Prevention of intestinal protozoan infections is common to all: drinking boiled water, washing fruit and vegetables, washing hands before meals and after the toilet, fly control, examining food workers and treating carriers.

cases.title: Case 1
cases.text: Workers who spent 2 months surveying gas fields in the Kyzylkum desert developed slowly healing ulcers on the exposed parts of their bodies.
cases.ask: What can you say about the nature and origin of this disease?
cases.answer: This is the rural (zoonotic) type of cutaneous leishmaniasis — the agent is *Leishmania major*. In the natural focus the reservoir is gerbils and the vector is sandflies; they breed near burrows and bite exposed parts of the body at night. A papule appears at the bite site, then a wet ulcer that heals with a scar in a few months. Diagnosis: amastigotes in a smear from the edge of the ulcer. Prevention: nets, repellents, rodent control, vaccination.

cases.title: Case 2
cases.text: A person who had worked in equatorial Africa developed drowsiness, weakness and headache that are getting worse.
cases.ask: What disease could this be? Is it contagious to others?
cases.answer: African trypanosomiasis (sleeping sickness), caused by *Trypanosoma brucei gambiense* or *T. b. rhodesiense*. The parasite multiplies first in the blood and lymph and then in the central nervous system, causing drowsiness, weakness and encephalitis. Diagnosis: smears of blood, lymph node aspirate and cerebrospinal fluid. It is not transmitted directly from person to person — only by the tsetse fly (vector-borne); since there are no tsetse flies in Uzbekistan, it will not spread to others.

cases.title: Case 3
cases.text: A pregnant woman had a spontaneous abortion. Parasites 4–7 µm long and 2–4 µm wide, shaped like a crescent or an orange segment, were found in the abortion material.
cases.ask: What caused the death of the fetus?
cases.answer: This is *Toxoplasma gondii* — congenital toxoplasmosis. The woman was infected for the first time during pregnancy (through oocysts in cat feces or cysts in undercooked meat); the parasite crossed the placenta into the fetus, damaged its tissues and caused its death. Prevention: serological testing before pregnancy, thorough cooking of meat, not handling cat litter without gloves, washing fruit and vegetables.

blocks.text: **Flatworms (Plathelminthes)** are bilaterally symmetrical, triploblastic animals with a dorsoventrally flattened body. They have no body cavity — the spaces between organs are filled with **parenchyma**. The body is covered by a **dermo-muscular sac**. The digestive system is blind (no anus; in tapeworms it is absent altogether), the excretory system consists of **protonephridia**, and the nervous system of paired cerebral ganglia and nerve cords. Most are **hermaphrodites**. The classes of medical importance are the flukes (**Trematoda**) and the tapeworms (**Cestoda**).

**Class Trematoda** — leaf-shaped parasites with an **oral** and a **ventral sucker**; the gut is blind and has two branches. Development involves a change of hosts: the definitive host is a vertebrate or a human, and the first intermediate host is always a **mollusc**. Larval stages: egg → **miracidium** (ciliated, swims in water) → **sporocyst** → **redia** → **cercaria** (tailed, leaves the mollusc) → **metacercaria** or **adolescaria** (the infective stage).

blocks.text: **Opisthorchiasis** is widespread in the Ob–Irtysh basin (Western Siberia) and along the Volga and Dnieper. Humans become infected by eating cyprinid fish (carp bream, ide, roach) containing metacercariae that are undercooked or lightly salted (Figure 12.2). The parasite damages the bile and pancreatic ducts, causing cholangitis, cholecystitis, pancreatitis and liver cirrhosis, and raises the risk of **cholangiocarcinoma**. Diagnosis — small (≈ 30 µm) operculated eggs in the faeces and duodenal fluid.

Kholikov et al., 2022).

parts.text: **Transit eggs:** a person who has eaten the liver of an animal infected with Fasciola (for example, liver kebab) may pass liver fluke eggs in the faeces for 1–2 days — this is **false fascioliasis**. To distinguish it from true infection, the patient is re-examined after 3–5 days on a liver-free diet.

blocks.text: **Tapeworms (Cestoda)** have a ribbon-like body consisting of a **scolex** (head with suckers, sometimes hooks, or sucking grooves — bothria), a **neck** (growth zone) and a **strobila** (a chain of segments — proglottids). There is no digestive system — nutrients are absorbed through the whole body surface. Each segment is hermaphroditic: in immature segments the reproductive organs develop, in **hermaphroditic** segments fertilization takes place, and in **gravid** segments only the uterus filled with eggs remains.

The egg contains a six-hooked embryo — the **oncosphere**. In the intermediate host the oncosphere develops into a larva — the **metacestode** (finna). Types of metacestode: the **cysticercus** (a vesicle with a single scolex — in Taenia), the **cysticercoid** (tailed, in the dwarf tapeworm), the **hydatid cyst** (with many scolices and daughter cysts), the **alveococcus** (a mass of many small vesicles that grows like a tumour), and the **procercoid** and **plerocercoid** (in the broad fish tapeworm).

parts.text: **Cysticercosis** develops when a person with taeniasis swallows the eggs themselves (dirty hands, gravid segments entering the stomach during vomiting — autoinfection) or infects others. Cysticerci in the brain cause seizures and hydrocephalus. Therefore a patient with taeniasis must be treated urgently and the people around them examined.

blocks.text: **Echinococcus** (*Echinococcus granulosus*) is a small tapeworm 3–6 mm long with 3–4 segments; its scolex has 4 suckers and hooks. The adult lives in the intestine of the **dog**, wolf and jackal. The eggs are passed in the faeces and contaminate the dog's fur, grass, water and vegetables. The intermediate hosts are sheep, cattle, camels, pigs and **humans**: in the intestine the oncospheres hatch and travel in the blood to the **liver** (≈ 70 %), **lungs** (≈ 20 %) and other organs, where a slowly growing **hydatid cyst** forms (Figure 12.4).

blocks.label: Figure 12.4

Kholikov et al., 2022).

blocks.text: The hydatid cyst consists of an outer chitin-like (laminated) layer and an inner **germinal** layer; it is filled with fluid, **daughter cysts** and numerous scolices (“hydatid sand”). The cyst compresses the surrounding tissue and impairs organ function; rupture can cause anaphylactic shock and the formation of many new cysts. Treatment is mainly surgical.

**Alveococcus** (*Alveococcus multilocularis*) — its definitive hosts are the fox, arctic fox and dog; its metacestode is a mass of small vesicles that **grows infiltratively like a tumour** in the liver and metastasizes; it runs a more severe course than echinococcosis. Humans become infected when handling fox pelts or eating unwashed wild berries.

parts.text: In echinococcosis **the human is a biological dead end**: the parasite does not pass from human cysts to another host. Humans are infected **only by swallowing eggs**; eating undercooked meat or liver does not transmit echinococcosis. Prevention: regular deworming of dogs, not feeding the infected internal organs of slaughtered animals to dogs, and washing hands after contact with dogs.

sections.title: 4. The dwarf tapeworm and the broad fish tapeworm

blocks.text: **The dwarf tapeworm** (*Hymenolepis nana*) is 1–5 cm long; the human is both the definitive and the intermediate host. After the eggs are swallowed, a **cysticercoid** develops in the villi of the small intestine, then emerges into the intestinal lumen and matures. Hundreds or thousands of parasites can accumulate in one person (**autoreinfection**). It spreads mainly in children's institutions by the contact-household route.

**The broad fish tapeworm** (*Diphyllobothrium latum*) is the longest human helminth (10 m or more); its scolex bears two sucking grooves (**bothria**); its segments are wider than they are long, and the uterus is rosette-shaped. Development takes place in water: a **coracidium** hatches from the egg → **procercoid** in the 1st intermediate host (Cyclops) → **plerocercoid** in the muscles and roe of the 2nd intermediate host (a predatory fish) → humans are infected by eating undercooked fish or salted roe. In the intestine the parasite takes up vitamin B~12~, causing **B~12~-deficiency (megaloblastic) anaemia**.

skills.title: Skill: identifying the tapeworm species from a gravid segment

items: Wash the segment separated from the faeces with water and press it between two glass slides.
Hold it up to the light or look under a magnifier at the central stem and lateral branches of the uterus (if necessary, inject ink or carmine).
Count the number of lateral branches on one side.
If there are 7–12 — conclude *Taenia solium*; if there are 17–35 — *Taeniarhynchus saginatus*.
Follow safety precautions: pork tapeworm eggs are dangerous to humans (cysticercosis) — work in gloves and disinfect the material.

cases.title: Case 1
cases.text: A man returning from a business trip to Siberia has signs of disease of the liver and bile ducts. Ovohelminthoscopic examination finds small operculated helminth eggs in his faeces.
cases.ask: What disease could this be?
cases.answer: The most likely diagnosis is opisthorchiasis (agent *Opisthorchis felineus*). Western Siberia (the Ob–Irtysh basin) is the world's largest focus of opisthorchiasis; humans are infected by eating cyprinid fish containing metacercariae that are undercooked, dried or lightly salted. The parasite lives in the bile ducts, gallbladder and pancreatic ducts. Confirmation — eggs in the duodenal fluid, serology; treatment — praziquantel.

cases.title: Case 2
cases.text: Tapeworm segments were found in a patient's faeces. When the lateral uterine branches were counted, there were 30 on one side.
cases.ask: What diagnosis can be made?
cases.answer: 17–35 pairs of lateral uterine branches are typical of the beef tapeworm (*Taeniarhynchus saginatus*) — taeniarhynchosis. The patient ate undercooked beef containing cysticerci. Unlike the pork tapeworm, this species does not cause cysticercosis in humans. Confirmation is the active emergence of segments and eggs in a perianal scraping; treatment — praziquantel or niclosamide.

cases.title: Case 3
cases.text: Can Echinococcus be transmitted to humans by eating undercooked kebab and liver kebab?
cases.ask: Justify your answer.
cases.answer: No. The hydatid cysts (metacestodes) in the meat or liver of sheep and cattle are infective only for the definitive host — dogs and other canids: when they eat infected internal organs, the adult worm develops in their intestine. Humans are intermediate hosts and become infected only by swallowing eggs passed in dog faeces (from fur, dirty hands, unwashed vegetables). However, other helminthiases (taeniarhynchosis, taeniasis) can be transmitted through undercooked meat.

goals.text: To teach the student the general features of the phylum Nemathelminthes and the class Nematoda, the concepts of geohelminths and biohelminths, the structure, life cycle, routes of transmission, pathogenic effects, diagnosis and prevention of the main nematodes that parasitize humans, and the methods of detecting helminth eggs.
By the end of the class the student should know:

items: the general features of nematodes and the concepts of geohelminth and biohelminth;
the types of infection: autoinfection, reinfection, autoreinfection, active and passive infection;
ascariasis, enterobiasis, trichuriasis, hookworm disease, strongyloidiasis, trichinellosis, dracunculiasis and the filariases;
the methods of ovohelminthoscopy and the concepts of dehelminthization and devastation.

goals.text: The student should be able to:

items: identify nematodes and their eggs in preparations;
prepare a direct smear and take a perianal scraping;
state the route of transmission and preventive measures for each nematode infection.

blocks.text: **Roundworms (Nemathelminthes)** are animals with a spindle-shaped or thread-like body that is round in cross-section and not divided into segments. The body is covered by a dense **cuticle**, beneath which lie the hypodermis and longitudinal muscles. They have a **primary body cavity (pseudocoel)** filled with fluid that acts as a hydroskeleton. The digestive system ends with an **anus** (fore-, mid- and hindgut). There are no circulatory or respiratory systems. Nematodes have **separate sexes** and marked sexual dimorphism: the male is smaller and its tail end is curved.

By type of development, helminths fall into two groups. **Geohelminths** develop without an intermediate host — their eggs or larvae mature **in the soil** (Ascaris, whipworm, hookworm). **Biohelminths** develop with the participation of an intermediate host (Trichinella, guinea worm, filariae, and all flukes and tapeworms). **Contact helminths** (pinworm, dwarf tapeworm) hardly mature in the environment at all and are transmitted via dirty hands and objects.

items: **Autoinfection** — the parasite reinfects the same organism without leaving it (dwarf tapeworm, strongyloidiasis).
**Reinfection** — repeated infection from outside.
**Autoreinfection** — swallowing one's own eggs again via the hands (pinworm).
**Active infection** — the larva enters through the skin by itself (hookworm, schistosomes); **passive infection** — via food, water or a vector.

sections.title: 2. The human roundworm and the pinworm

blocks.text: **The human roundworm** (*Ascaris lumbricoides*) is the agent of **ascariasis**, a geohelminth found everywhere. The female is 20–40 cm long, the male 15–25 cm; the mouth is surrounded by three lips. It lives in the small intestine; the female lays up to 200 thousand eggs a day. Eggs passed in the faeces are **not immediately infective** for humans — they mature in the soil over 2–3 weeks given oxygen, moisture and warmth (≈ 24 °C), and an infective larva develops inside.

blocks.label: Figure 13.1
blocks.caption: Life cycle of the human roundworm *Ascaris lumbricoides*: maturation of the eggs in soil, swallowing of the infective egg, larval migration (intestine → vein → liver → heart → lungs → alveoli → bronchi → trachea → pharynx → intestine) and maturation in the small intestine (P.Kh. Kholikov et al., 2022).

blocks.text: Humans swallow mature eggs with unwashed vegetables and fruit, dirty hands and water. Larvae hatching in the intestine pass through the gut wall into the blood and **migrate** (Figure 13.1), causing eosinophilic infiltrates in the lungs, cough and allergic reactions (**migratory phase**). The swallowed larvae mature in the small intestine within 2–3 months (**intestinal phase**): abdominal pain, weight loss, intestinal obstruction, blockage of the bile ducts. Diagnosis — eggs in the faeces; in the migratory phase, larvae in the sputum and eosinophilia.

**The pinworm** (*Enterobius vermicularis*) is the agent of **enterobiasis**, a contact helminth found mainly in children. The female is 9–12 mm long, the male 2–5 mm; they are white (Figure 13.2). It lives in the initial part of the large intestine. At night the females crawl out of the anus and lay eggs in the perianal folds, causing intense **itching**. The eggs become infective within 4–6 hours; when the child scratches, they get under the fingernails and are swallowed again (**autoreinfection**). Diagnosis — a **perianal scraping** or adhesive tape test in the morning; stool examination is ineffective.

blocks.label: Figure 13.2
blocks.caption: The pinworm *Enterobius vermicularis*: female (left) and male (right); the mouth, vesicle, oesophageal bulb, midgut, reproductive system, vulva and anus are shown (P.Kh. Kholikov et al., 2022).

sections.title: 3. The whipworm, the hookworm and the threadworm

blocks.text: **The whipworm** (*Trichocephalus trichiurus*) is the agent of **trichuriasis**, a geohelminth 3–5 cm long. The front part of its body is hair-thin, and with it the worm “stitches” itself into the mucosa of the caecum and colon and feeds on blood (Figure 13.3). Its eggs are **lemon-shaped** with plugs at both poles; they mature in the soil in 3–4 weeks. Heavy infection causes anaemia, colitis and, in children, rectal prolapse.

blocks.label: Figure 13.3
blocks.caption: The whipworm *Trichocephalus trichiurus*: male, female and egg (left); the worm with its thin anterior end embedded in the intestinal mucosa (right) (P.Kh. Kholikov et al., 2022).

blocks.text: **The Old World hookworm** (*Ancylostoma duodenale*) and **Necator** (*Necator americanus*) cause **hookworm disease**, which is common in hot, humid areas (mines, rice fields). They are 8–13 mm long, with cutting teeth or plates in the buccal capsule. In the soil a rhabditiform and then a **filariform** larva develops from the egg; it **actively** penetrates human skin (Figure 13.4), travels in the blood to the lungs, ascends to the pharynx, is swallowed and matures in the duodenum. The parasite sucks blood and injures the intestinal wall — severe **iron-deficiency anaemia** develops.

blocks.label: Figure 13.4
blocks.caption: Life cycle of the hookworm *Ancylostoma duodenale*: eggs passed in the faeces, rhabditiform and filariform larvae in the soil, entry through the skin, migration through the lungs and maturation in the small intestine (P.Kh. Kholikov et al., 2022).

blocks.text: **The threadworm** (*Strongyloides stercoralis*) is the agent of **strongyloidiasis**; it is ≈ 2 mm long. Transmission resembles that of hookworm (filariform larvae through the skin). Its special feature is **autoinfection** in the intestine, so the disease lasts for decades; when immunity is weakened (glucocorticoids, HIV), a severe disseminated form develops. Diagnosis — larvae in the faeces.

**Trichinella** (*Trichinella spiralis*) is the agent of **trichinellosis**; it is 1.5–4 mm long. One animal serves first as the definitive and then as the intermediate host. Humans are infected by eating undercooked **pork**, wild boar or bear meat containing larvae. In the small intestine the larvae mature and the females give birth to live larvae; these travel in the blood to the **striated muscles** (diaphragm, masticatory, intercostal and eye muscles), become encapsulated and remain alive for years. Signs: fever, **swelling of the face and eyelids**, severe muscle pain and marked **eosinophilia**. Diagnosis — serological tests, muscle biopsy, **trichinoscopy** of the remaining meat.

**The guinea worm** (*Dracunculus medinensis*) is the agent of **dracunculiasis**; the female is up to 120 cm long. Its intermediate host is the **Cyclops**. Humans are infected by drinking pond water containing Cyclops with larvae; the female worm settles in the subcutaneous tissue (usually of the legs), forms a blister on the skin and releases its larvae into the water when the leg touches water. **In Uzbekistan** the guinea worm was completely eradicated in 1932 as a result of measures led by L.M. Isaev — a classic example of **devastation**.

parts.text: In diagnosing the filariases, microfilariae are found in the blood; the microfilariae of *Wuchereria bancrofti* appear in the peripheral blood mainly **at night**, so the blood smear is taken at night.

blocks.text: **Ovohelminthoscopy** is the set of methods for finding helminth eggs and larvae. In the **macroscopic** method, adult worms and segments in the faeces are examined with the naked eye or a magnifier. **Microscopic** methods: the **direct smear** (a drop of faeces with glycerol or saline), the **Kato thick smear**, **sedimentation** methods (formalin-ether — for heavy eggs such as fluke eggs) and **flotation** methods (Fülleborn — light eggs float to the surface in saturated NaCl solution). Pinworm and beef tapeworm eggs are detected with a **perianal scraping** or adhesive tape (Figure 13.5).

blocks.label: Figure 13.5
blocks.caption: Eggs of parasitic worms: 1 — *Schistosoma haematobium*; 2 — *S. mansoni*; 3 — *Fasciola hepatica*; 4 — *S. japonicum*; 5 — *Paragonimus*; 6 — *Dicrocoelium lanceatum*; 7 — *Clonorchis sinensis*; 8 — *Opisthorchis felineus*; 9 — *Taeniarhynchus saginatus*; 10 — *Diphyllobothrium latum*; 11 — *Hymenolepis nana*; 12 — *H. diminuta*; 13 — *Trichocephalus trichiurus*; 14 — *Ascaris lumbricoides* (unfertilized, without the protein coat); 15 — *A. lumbricoides* (fertilized); 16 — *A. lumbricoides* (unfertilized, with the protein coat); 17 — *Enterobius vermicularis* (P.Kh. Kholikov et al., 2022).

blocks.text: **Dehelminthization** comprises the measures that rid the human body (treatment) and the environment (disinfection of faeces, protection of soil and water) of helminths and their eggs. **Devastation** — a term introduced by academician **K.I. Skryabin** — is the **complete extermination** of a helminth species in a given area at all of its stages (adult, larva, egg) by a combination of biological, chemical and organizational measures. Its aim is not to reduce disease but to eliminate the causative agent from the area.

skills.title: Skill: preparing a direct smear and taking a perianal scraping

items: Place a drop of 50 % glycerol or saline on a glass slide.
With a wooden stick take a match-head-sized sample from different parts of the faeces, spread it evenly in the drop and cover with a coverslip.
Examine the whole preparation first under the low-power and then the high-power objective; identify the eggs by shape, size, shell and operculum.
A perianal scraping is taken in the morning, before washing and defecation: material is collected from the perianal folds with a stick moistened in glycerol or with adhesive tape.
Stick the tape onto a slide and examine it under the microscope; pinworm eggs are asymmetrical, flattened on one side.

cases.title: Case 1
cases.text: It was found that toys in a kindergarten might be contaminated with Ascaris eggs.
cases.ask: Can such eggs cause ascariasis in the children?
cases.answer: Ascaris is a geohelminth: eggs freshly passed in the faeces are not infective; they become infective only after maturing in the soil over 2–3 weeks given oxygen, moisture and warmth. Therefore fresh eggs that reach a toy directly from a patient's faeces do not cause ascariasis. However, if the toys are contaminated with soil (a sandpit), it may contain mature infective eggs — in that case there is a risk of infection. Prevention: replacing the sand in sandpits, washing toys and teaching children to wash their hands.

cases.title: Case 2
cases.text: Small, motile, white worms were seen in a child's faeces. The mother complains that the child sleeps restlessly at night and scratches around the anus.
cases.ask: What parasitic disease can be suspected? What should be done to confirm it?
cases.answer: Enterobiasis is suspected (agent — the pinworm, *Enterobius vermicularis*): at night the female pinworms crawl out to the perianal area, lay eggs and cause itching. To confirm, material is taken in the morning, before washing, by perianal scraping or the adhesive tape method, and asymmetrical eggs are found under the microscope; the test is repeated 3 times. To stop autoreinfection, the child and family members are treated at the same time, the nails are cut short, and underwear is changed and ironed daily.

cases.title: Case 3
cases.text: A hunter shared wild boar meat with his fellow villagers. A few days later, most of those who ate the meat came to the clinic with facial swelling, fever and severe muscle pain.
cases.ask: What disease might the doctor suspect? How can the suspicion be confirmed?
cases.answer: Trichinellosis (agent — *Trichinella spiralis*). The encapsulated larvae in the wild boar meat mature in the intestine, and new larvae spread in the blood to the striated muscles — this causes fever, swelling of the face and eyelids, and myalgia. Group illness from a single source is typical. Confirmation: marked eosinophilia in the blood, serological tests (ELISA), muscle biopsy; trichinoscopy of the remaining meat. Prevention — veterinary inspection and thorough cooking of meat.

blocks.text: **Arthropods (Arthropoda)** are the largest phylum of the animal kingdom. General features: the body and legs are **jointed**, the external skeleton is a **chitinous** cuticle, growth takes place by **moulting**, the body cavity is mixed (**mixocoel**), and the circulatory system is open. Three subphyla matter for medicine: the **gill-breathers** (crustaceans — Cyclops and crabs are intermediate hosts of helminths), the **chelicerates** (arachnids) and the **tracheates** (insects).

**Arachnids (Arachnida)** have a body divided into a **cephalothorax** and an **abdomen**, 4 pairs of walking legs, chelicerae and pedipalps around the mouth, and no antennae. Of medical importance are scorpions, spiders and especially the order of **ticks and mites (Acari)**. Ticks and mites are divided into the **acariform** group (the scabies mite and the follicle mite — *Demodex*) and the **parasitiform** group (argasid and ixodid ticks). Tick development: egg → **larva** (3 pairs of legs) → **nymph** → **imago** (4 pairs of legs).

blocks.text: **Transovarial and transstadial transmission in ticks:** the pathogen multiplies in the tick and passes through the egg to the next generation (**transovarial**) and from larva to nymph and from nymph to imago (**transstadial**). Ticks are therefore not only vectors but also **natural reservoirs** of the pathogen. Academician **Ye.N. Pavlovsky** developed the doctrine of the **natural focality** of vector-borne diseases: the pathogen circulates among wild animals and vectors independently of humans.

**The scabies mite** (*Sarcoptes scabiei*) is the agent of **scabies**; it measures 0.3–0.4 mm. The female burrows tunnels in the stratum corneum of the skin and lays her eggs there. Favourite sites are the spaces between the fingers, the wrists, abdomen and inner thighs. The main sign is **itching that worsens at night**. Transmission — direct skin contact, shared bedding and clothing. Diagnosis — finding the mite in a scraping taken from a burrow.

sections.title: 2. Class Insecta. Lice, fleas, bedbugs, cockroaches

blocks.text: **Insects (Insecta)** have a body consisting of a **head**, **thorax** and **abdomen**; the thorax bears 3 pairs of legs and usually 2 pairs of wings, and the head 1 pair of antennae; they breathe through tracheae. Development is of two kinds: with **incomplete metamorphosis** (egg → larva → imago: lice, bedbugs, cockroaches) and with **complete metamorphosis** (egg → larva → **pupa** → imago: fleas, Diptera).

**Lice (Anoplura)** are wingless permanent ectoparasites that feed only on human blood throughout their life (Figure 14.2). Three species parasitize humans: the **head louse** (*Pediculus humanus capitis*), the **body louse** (*P. h. corporis*) and the **pubic louse** (*Phthirus pubis*). A louse feeds 2–3 times a day for 3–10 minutes each time; the female lays 6–14 eggs (nits) a day, gluing them to hair or clothing fibres; development from egg to imago takes 16–20 days. Louse infestation is called **pediculosis**.

blocks.label: Figure 14.2
blocks.caption: Lice: a — male head louse; b — female head louse; c — pubic louse clinging to a hair; d — louse engorged with blood (P.Kh. Kholikov et al., 2022).

parts.text: **The body louse** is the vector of epidemic **typhus** (*Rickettsia prowazekii*) and epidemic **relapsing fever** (*Borrelia recurrentis*). The pathogens are not transmitted with saliva when the louse bites: in typhus the rickettsiae are passed in the louse's **faeces** and rubbed into scratched skin; in relapsing fever the borreliae are in the louse's haemolymph and enter skin wounds **when the louse is crushed**. In wars, famine and breakdowns of hygiene these diseases become epidemic.

blocks.text: **Fleas (Siphonaptera)** are wingless insects, flattened from side to side, with jumping legs; they develop with complete metamorphosis, and their larvae live in floor cracks and rubbish. **The rat flea** (*Xenopsylla cheopis*) is the vector of **plague** (*Yersinia pestis*): the bacteria form a “block” in the flea's proventriculus and are regurgitated into the wound when it feeds. **The human flea** (*Pulex irritans*) can also carry plague.

**The bedbug** (*Cimex lectularius*) feeds at night, and its bites cause itching and allergy. **Cockroaches** (*Blattella germanica, Periplaneta americana*) are **mechanical carriers** of intestinal infections, helminth eggs and protozoan cysts; their chitin remains and secretions are strong **allergens** that cause bronchial asthma and allergic reactions in children.

**Diptera** are insects with one pair of membranous wings, the second pair having become vibrating halteres; they develop with complete metamorphosis. They are divided into two suborders: the **long-horned** (mosquitoes, sandflies, black flies — *Simulium*) and the **short-horned** (flies, horseflies).

blocks.text: ***Aedes*** mosquitoes carry the dengue, yellow fever and Zika viruses. **Sandflies** (*Phlebotomus*) are small and hairy and breed in rodent burrows in hot regions; they are the vectors of the **leishmaniases** (cutaneous and visceral) and of sandfly (pappataci) fever. **Black flies** (*Simulium*) carry onchocerciasis.

**The housefly** (*Musca domestica*) is a **mechanical carrier** of intestinal infections (dysentery, typhoid fever, cholera), helminth eggs and protozoan cysts: microbes are carried on the sticky hairs of its feet, on its proboscis and in its gut, and reach food in vomit and faeces. **Wohlfahrt's fly** (*Wohlfahrtia magnifica*) deposits live larvae in wounds, ears, nose and eyes — causing **obligate myiasis**. **The stable fly** (*Stomoxys calcitrans*) and **horseflies** (*Tabanidae*) suck blood but are only **mechanical** carriers of anthrax and tularaemia. **The tsetse fly** (*Glossina*) carries sleeping sickness (trypanosomiasis) in Africa.

items: **Specific (biological) vector** — the pathogen multiplies in it or completes part of its life cycle there (Anopheles — malaria, sandfly — Leishmania, louse — rickettsia, tick — encephalitis virus).
**Mechanical carrier** — the pathogen stays unchanged in the carrier and is merely transferred on its body surface or proboscis (housefly, cockroach, horsefly, stable fly).

blocks.text: **Venomous animals** produce or accumulate substances that are toxic to humans and animals. **Primarily venomous** animals produce venom in special glands themselves; they are either **actively armed** (with a venom gland and a stinging or biting apparatus: snakes, scorpions, spiders, wasps) or **passive** (with venom glands but no delivery apparatus: frogs, some fish). **Secondarily venomous** animals accumulate toxins from their food (some fish and molluscs). By their action, venoms are **neurotoxic** (acting on the nervous system) or **haemotoxic** (acting on the blood and vessels).

cases.title: Case 1
cases.text: Scabies was found in most of the students sent to pick cotton.
cases.ask: Explain the reasons. What measures can eliminate the disease?
cases.answer: The scabies mite, *Sarcoptes scabiei*, is transmitted by direct skin contact, shared beds, bedding and clothing. Crowded living in dormitories, sleeping on shared bedding and limited opportunities to wash and change clothes caused the disease to spread quickly. Measures: treating all patients and their contacts at the same time (permethrin, benzyl benzoate), boiling or hot-ironing underwear and bedding, isolating patients, examining contacts and improving sanitary and hygienic conditions.

cases.title: Case 2
cases.text: A tick taken from an animal was examined under the microscope: no chitinous scutum was found on its back, and its mouthparts are not visible from above. Among other ticks, there are also specimens in which the pathogen was found even though they had not fed on blood.
cases.ask: Which family does this tick belong to? How can the presence of the pathogen in ticks that have not fed be explained?
cases.answer: The absence of a scutum and the position of the mouthparts on the underside of the body are typical of argasid ticks (*Argasidae*), for example the village tick — the vector of tick-borne relapsing fever. The pathogen in unfed ticks is explained by transovarial transmission: the pathogen multiplies in the mother tick and passes through the egg to the next generation, and it is also retained from larva to nymph and imago by the transstadial route. Ticks are therefore natural reservoirs of the pathogen.

cases.title: Case 3
cases.text: A person bitten by a snake has bleeding from the bite site, severe pain, rapidly spreading swelling and a sharp fall in blood pressure. Another patient, after a snakebite, developed difficulty breathing and swallowing, numbness of the body and difficulty moving.
cases.ask: In each case, what kind of snake might be suspected?
cases.answer: The first case shows the effect of a haemotoxic venom — impaired blood clotting, damage to the vessel walls and local tissue necrosis; this is seen after bites by vipers such as the Levant viper (gyurza), the saw-scaled viper or the Halys pit viper. The second case shows the effect of a neurotoxic venom — blockade of neuromuscular transmission, paralysis and respiratory failure; this is seen after a bite by the Central Asian cobra. In both cases the limb is immobilized, no tourniquet is applied, and the patient is taken urgently to hospital and given snake antivenom; in neurotoxic poisoning one must be ready for artificial ventilation.

topics.title: Onto-phylogenesis of organ systems: skin, skeleton, nervous system, circulation, endocrine system, excretory system. Ecology. The human as an ecological factor. The biosphere and its problems

goals.text: To teach the student the main lines of evolution of the organ systems of vertebrates, the phylogenetic causes of congenital defects found in humans (atavisms, rudiments), as well as the basics of ecology, the role of humans as an ecological factor and the problems of the biosphere.
By the end of the class the student should know:

items: the concepts of homologous and analogous organs, rudiments and atavisms;
the evolution of the integumentary, skeletal, circulatory, nervous, excretory, digestive, respiratory and endocrine systems;
the phylogenetically determined congenital defects found in humans;
the ecological factors, the doctrine of the biosphere and noosphere, and the genetic consequences of environmental pollution.

goals.text: The student should be able to:

items: compare the heart, arterial arches and brain of vertebrates of different classes;
explain whether a congenital defect is linked to the recurrence of an ancestral feature or to the disruption of an embryonic process.

blocks.text: The evolution of organs is studied by **evolutionary morphology** on the basis of data from **comparative anatomy**, **comparative embryology** and **palaeontology**. **Homologous organs** have the same origin and structural plan but may have different functions (the pectoral fin of a fish, the wing of a bird, the human arm). **Analogous organs** have the same function but a different origin (the wings of a butterfly and of a bird).

**Rudiments** are vestigial organs that have lost their function in evolution and are retained in all people (the vermiform appendix, the coccygeal vertebrae, the muscles of the auricle, the semilunar fold of the eye). **Atavisms** are the reappearance of features of distant ancestors in individual people (a tail, hair covering the whole body — hypertrichosis, extra nipples — polymastia, cervical fistulae). Most atavisms result from structures present in the embryo failing to be remodelled in time: according to the **biogenetic law** (F. Müller, E. Haeckel), ontogenesis is a brief recapitulation of phylogenesis.

parts.text: Phylogenetically determined defects in humans arise by two mechanisms: 1) **persistence** of an embryonic structure (tail, cervical fistulae, patent ductus arteriosus); 2) **arrest** of organ development at an ancestral stage (three-chambered heart, pelvic kidney, right aortic arch).

sections.title: 2. The integument, skeleton, digestive and respiratory systems

blocks.text: **Integument.** In invertebrates the skin consists of a single-layered epithelium and a cuticle. In vertebrates the skin has two layers: the stratified **epidermis** develops from ectoderm and the **dermis** from mesoderm. Skin derivatives change from class to class: bony and **placoid scales** in fish (their homologue is the teeth of mammals), mucous glands in amphibians, horny scales in reptiles, feathers in birds, and hair, sweat, sebaceous and **mammary glands** in mammals. Anomalies: **ichthyosis** (a hereditary disorder of the horny layer, in which the skin comes to resemble fish scales), hypertrichosis, polymastia (extra nipples along the milk lines).

**Skeleton.** In the lancelet the axial skeleton is the **notochord**; in vertebrates it is replaced by the vertebral column. The skull consists of the braincase and the **visceral skeleton** derived from the gill arches (the auditory ossicles, the hyoid bone and the laryngeal cartilages are derivatives of the gill arches). The five-digit limb arose from the fin of lobe-finned fish. Anomalies: cervical ribs, **spina bifida**, polydactyly, syndactyly, **Sprengel's deformity** (failure of the scapula to descend from its embryonic position in the neck).

**Digestive and respiratory systems.** In the evolution of the gut tube we see its division into sections, its lengthening and the appearance of digestive glands. Only mammals form a **secondary palate**; failure of it to close is **cleft palate**. In the embryo the gut tube is temporarily occluded and then reopened (**recanalization**); if this process is disrupted, **atresia and stenosis** of the oesophagus, duodenum or intestine result. The respiratory organs develop from the gill pouches and from an outgrowth of the floor of the pharynx: gills in fish, lungs in land vertebrates, alveolar lungs in mammals. Anomalies: **tracheo-oesophageal fistula**, aplasia of a lung or a lung lobe.

The line of evolution is the **improvement of the heart** and the **separation of arterial and venous blood**. **The lancelet** has no heart; blood is moved by contractions of the ventral aorta, and there is one circulation. **In fish** the heart has two chambers (atrium and ventricle) and contains only venous blood; there is one circulation. **In amphibians** the heart has three chambers (two atria and one ventricle), there are two circulations, and blood **mixes** in the ventricle. **In reptiles** the ventricle has an incomplete septum (complete in crocodiles), and two aortic arches are retained. **In birds** and **mammals** the heart has four chambers and the blood does not mix: birds retain the **right** aortic arch and mammals the **left**.

When arterial and venous blood mix, cyanosis, breathlessness and delayed physical development are seen.

sections.title: 4. The nervous, excretory and endocrine systems

blocks.text: **Nervous system.** In invertebrates the nervous system evolved from **diffuse** (Hydra) → **ladder-like** (flatworms) → **ventral nerve cord** (annelids, arthropods). In vertebrates the central nervous system forms from the **neural tube**; the brain has five parts: the forebrain, diencephalon, midbrain, cerebellum and medulla oblongata (Figure 15.2). Three brain types are distinguished: **ichthyopsid** (fish, amphibians — the highest integrating centre is the midbrain), **sauropsid** (reptiles, birds — the striate bodies of the forebrain) and **mammalian** (mammals — the **new cortex**, neocortex). Anomalies: anencephaly, microcephaly, hydrocephalus, spinal hernia.

Kholikov et al., 2022).

blocks.text: **Excretory system.** In invertebrates — protonephridia (flatworms), metanephridia (annelids), Malpighian tubules (insects). In vertebrates the kidney is replaced in three stages: the **head kidney (pronephros)** — in cyclostomes and the embryos of all vertebrates; the **trunk (primary) kidney (mesonephros)** — in fish and amphibians; the **pelvic (secondary) kidney (metanephros)** — in reptiles, birds and mammals. All three stages also follow one another in the human embryo. Anomalies: renal aplasia, **horseshoe kidney**, a kidney remaining in the pelvis (dystopia), duplex kidney, polycystic disease.

**Endocrine system.** Hormonal regulation began with neurosecretion; in vertebrates the hypothalamic-pituitary system takes the central place. The thyroid gland develops from the floor of the pharynx and is homologous with the **endostyle** of the lancelet; the cortex and medulla of the adrenal gland are separate in fish and unite in land vertebrates. Insufficiency of the adrenal cortex is **Addison's disease**: hyperpigmentation of the skin and mucous membranes, weight loss and disturbed water-salt metabolism.

sections.title: 5. Ecology. The human as an ecological factor. The biosphere

blocks.text: **Ecology** (the term was introduced by E. Haeckel in 1866) is the science of the relationships of organisms with one another and with their environment. Its branches: autecology (a single species), population ecology, synecology (communities) and **human ecology**. **Ecological factors**: **abiotic** (temperature, light, humidity, ionizing radiation), **biotic** (the influence of other organisms — parasitism, symbiosis, competition) and **anthropogenic** (human activity). An organism lives within a certain **range of tolerance** for each factor; the factor that deviates most from the optimum becomes the **limiting factor**.

**The biosphere** is the shell of the Earth inhabited by living organisms and transformed by them (the lower atmosphere, the hydrosphere and the upper lithosphere). The doctrine of the biosphere was created by **V.I. Vernadsky**: living matter is the main driving force of the cycling of substances on the planet. Human activity is creating a new state of the biosphere — the **noosphere** (sphere of reason). Current problems: pollution of the air, water and soil, the greenhouse effect, depletion of the ozone layer, desertification and loss of biodiversity; for Uzbekistan — the **Aral Sea** disaster and its effect on public health.

parts.text: **Genetic consequences of environmental pollution:** chemical mutagens (pesticides, heavy metals, benzpyrene), ionizing radiation and some viruses increase the mutation rate — this leads to more hereditary diseases, congenital defects, infertility and tumours. **Genetic monitoring** of the population and control of mutagens are therefore necessary.

blocks.text: **The human as an ecological factor.** Unlike other organisms, humans consciously change their environment. This ability was formed during the long process of **anthropogenesis** (Figure 15.3): dryopithecines → australopithecines → **handy man** (*Homo habilis*, the first tools) → **archanthropes** (Pithecanthropus, Sinanthropus) → **palaeoanthropes** (Neanderthals) → **neoanthropes** (Cro-Magnons, *Homo sapiens*). Alongside the biological factors of anthropogenesis (natural selection, variation), social factors — labour, speech and life in groups — played the decisive role.

cases.title: Case 1
cases.text: In a maternity hospital a baby was born with its body covered in hair and with a tail.
cases.ask: Explain this anomaly.
cases.answer: Both features are atavisms — the reappearance of features of distant ancestors. In weeks 4–6 the human embryo has a tail bud, which then regresses, leaving the coccygeal vertebrae (a rudiment); if regression is disrupted, the baby is born with a tail. The fine hair covering the fetal body (lanugo) is normally shed before birth; if it persists or is strongly developed, hypertrichosis is seen. The mechanism is the failure of embryonic structures to be remodelled in time (the biogenetic law).

cases.title: Case 2
cases.text: A newborn has congenital openings (fistulae) on the neck.
cases.ask: Explain how this anomaly develops.
cases.answer: These are cervical (branchial) fistulae — a phylogenetically determined defect. In the human embryo, as in the gill apparatus of fish, gill pouches form in the wall of the pharynx and gill clefts in the skin of the neck. Normally they close and turn into various structures (the middle ear cavity, the auditory tube, the tonsils, the parathyroid glands). If the gill clefts or pouches do not close completely, fistulae and cysts remain on the side of the neck. Treatment is surgical.

cases.title: Case 3
cases.text: A two-year-old child has bluish skin, breathes rapidly and has a body temperature below normal. The clinic diagnosed a “heart defect”, but the heart valves are normally formed.
cases.ask: What abnormalities of the heart or blood vessels lead to these changes?
cases.answer: With normal valves, the cyanosis is due to mixing of arterial and venous blood: a ventricular or atrial septal defect (a structure resembling the amphibian and reptilian heart — arrest of development at an ancestral stage), patent ductus arteriosus (persistence of an embryonic vessel), transposition of the great arteries or tetralogy of Fallot. Lack of oxygen in the tissues leads to cyanosis, breathlessness, weakness and delayed development. Diagnosis — echocardiography; treatment — cardiac surgery.
